Zine No. 15 Every Creature's Own Sky Stimpunks Zines Umwelt as star stuff. Every creature is sealed in its own complete perceptual world — the tick's three signals, the bat's echo, the mantis shrimp's light, the dog's scent-time — and each world is whole, not a partial view of one real world underneath. There is no neutral, default way to sense. The animals do the arguing, so that when minds enter, the point lands as recognition: monotropism is an attention-world, Autistic perception a different and complete sky, not a broken copy of a standard one. And when two worlds meet — human and bat, one mind and another — the gap is mutual: the double empathy problem, arrived at without lecturing. Not one correct channel, but mutual translation. Carries the Umwelt thread from No. 14 inward, from von Uexküll through Tarragnat, Manning, Milton, and Despret. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads→

Zine No. 16 Minor Worlds Stimpunks Zines Niche construction as star stuff, and the third of a loose trilogy — how we treat other worlds (No. 14), how we sense them (No. 15), and here, how we build them. Organisms don't just adapt to a fixed environment; they remake it — the beaver's dam, the spider's web — and pass the built world on as ecological inheritance. So the neurodiversity turn is plain: don't fix the mind, change the environment (positive niche construction — there is no “normal” brain in a vat). Stimming is worldmaking; minor worlds and niche communities are real, not lesser; and no niche is neutral — the “default” room was built for one kind of mind, so the fix is reconstruction, not accommodation. Grounded in Odling-Smee & Laland, Armstrong, Tarragnat, Manning, Kadodia & Krueger, and Haraway, and rooted in Stimpunks' own glossary. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads→

Zine No. 17 The Nearest Body Stimpunks Zines Tides and co-regulation as star stuff. The Sun out-masses the Moon 27 million times, yet the Moon runs the tide — because tidal force falls off with the cube of distance, and nearness beats mass. So co-regulation is gravity: a safe-enough nervous system nearby pulls yours into rhythm, at a distance, without touching. Spring and neap tides as aligned or crossed pulls, parallel presence as tidal locking, meerkat mode as a sea that lost its moon, and the ecosystemic turn — the storm is in the weather, not the water. Grounded in the Stimpunks glossary (co-regulation, polyvagal theory, meerkat mode, ARLES, regulation-first), with a hydrofeminist thread carried inward from No. 14. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads→

Zine No. 18 The Garden and the Stars Stimpunks Zines Knowledge gardening as star stuff — a self-portrait of the whole project. If stimpunks.org is the knowledge garden, starstuff.earth is where it flowers, and these zines are the blooms. A garden, not a stream: evergreen, cross-linked, walkable, grown from lived experience rather than handed down as hierarchy (a rhizome and a mycelial network, after Deleuze & Guattari). The cosmic turn: a knowledge garden is how star stuff comes to know itself — a supernova scatters its forged elements like a seed-head (SN 1006, liberating iron), and the universe knows itself not as a vault but as a garden, by growing and seeding. Held in common, not enclosed: CC BY-SA, print free, share freely — the licence line is the seed dispersal. Grounded in Caulfield, Appleton, Bush, Deleuze & Guattari, Ostrom, and Sagan, and rooted in Stimpunks' own garden and commons. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a cover bed of blooms keyed to the prior zines' colours, a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads→

Zine No. 19 No Universal Now Stimpunks Zines Crip time, read through relativity — with a guest coda by Helen Edgar. Physics says there is no universal “now”: simultaneity is relative and clocks run at different rates by speed and gravity (your phone's GPS corrects for it). So the one true clock is a human invention — railway-and-factory standard time, a convention we mistook for a law and then began grading bodies and minds against. Crip time (Zola & Gill, Kafer, Samuels, Price) bends the clock back to fit us instead of bending us to it — the same move as Minor Worlds, now applied to time. Monotropic spiral time and felt time (Helen Edgar, Bergson, Deleuze) are their own real clock, measured in intensity, not minutes; Samuels' time travel, grief time, and broken time hold the hard edges too. The reading: no clock is master, and being “off the clock” is closer to the truth than fitting it. Nine spreads, seven diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set, and a closing coda by Helen Edgar on spiral time. 9 spreads→

Zine No. 20 The Same Water Stimpunks Zines Fluctuating capacity, read through the physics of phase transitions. Water doesn't get gradually stiffer as it cools — it holds, then flips to ice all at once at a threshold. Same H₂O, different state, and the conditions (not the substance) decide which. So the exhausting question — why could you do it yesterday and not today? — has a clean answer: capacity is a state, not a trait, and you were near a boundary. The hardest part is the crossing itself (threshold anxiety is sensitivity to a real edge — broken thresholds, not broken people); you can be supercooled, held past your limit until one small thing tips everything at once; and recovery slows near the edge, because that's how systems behave. Nothing is fixed or broken — fluid adaptation and weather-bodies, re-adapting to a changed climate. Extends Minor Worlds: change the conditions, not the substance. Grounded in phase-transition physics, Cynthia Kim, Helen Edgar, and Stimpunks' own threshold anxiety. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads→

Zine No. 21 Not a Line Stimpunks Zines The spectrum was never a severity scale — after Helen Edgar & Patrick Dwyer. “Spectrum” is the most misread word in our vocabulary: people hear a line from mild to severe. But a real spectrum isn't a ladder — split a star's light and every element signs its own pattern of lines, a fingerprint, which is the only way we know what stars are made of. And the sky's figure was never a line: it's a constellation. The zine follows the escalation from Helen Edgar's brand-new essay — the line of neuronormativity, to the spiky profile (better, but still a grid measured from a baseline), to a constellation of intensities: no rank, no norm, no line. Patrick Dwyer's autism constellation anchors it; the functioning-labels critique shows how the line gatekeeps support (“not disabled enough” vs “too disabled”). Held with care: refusing the line doesn't erase that some of us need far more support — need is not a rank; name it instead. Cashes in the rainbow motif on every page and hands off to the Constellation Field Guide. Eight spreads, spectrum-forward diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads→

Zine No. 22 No One Is the Leader Stimpunks Zines Emergence and the murmuration — a flock has no captain, and neither does a self. Hundreds of thousands of starlings make vast rolling shapes with no leader and no plan: each bird tracks only its six or seven nearest neighbours (Ballerini & the STARFLAG project), and the whole emerges from that one local rule. Philip Anderson's “More Is Different” (1972) is the spine — the founding statement of anti-reductionism: at each level of scale new laws appear that the parts don't contain, so knowing the parts never rebuilds the whole. The early universe did the same, self-organising faint density ripples into the cosmic web with no architect. Two payoffs land it home: the whole person is realer than any diagnostic checklist of parts (you are not a list of deficits — you are the murmuration), and our best neurodivergent collectives — NeurodiVentures — are leaderless murmurations, not org charts (competency networks and catalysts rather than leaders; decisions where the knowledge lives). A “the whole exceeds the parts” zine. Held with care: leaderless is not structureless. Eight spreads, flock-and-web diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads→

Zine No. 23 Bodies of Water Stimpunks Zines Hydrofeminism as belonging, read through star stuff — after Astrida Neimanis. You are not a container of water; you are water, roughly 60% of you, briefly gathered into a shape. And none of it is only yours: it was rain, river, cloud, and the inside of other creatures first. Neimanis's gestationality (we each began inside another body's water) and Stacy Alaimo's transcorporeality dissolve the clean edge — we are all downstream of one another, permeable and borrowed. The crucial move, held with care: watery belonging is not dissolution into sameness. Where two rivers meet, the confluence runs braided for miles — one channel, two waters, still distinct. That's the neurodiversity paradigm in an image: the spiky profile survives the merge. A dedicated spread carries shared/collective flow — monotropism's deep channels can align into shared flow (Autistic Realms, Helen Edgar); a watering hole is where currents pool. So belonging is a current, not a border — build watering holes, keep the water moving. Much of Earth's water is older than the Sun. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads→

Zine No. 24 Shared Air Stimpunks Zines The air we share, read through star stuff and solarpunk — a companion to Bodies of Water. There is only one air: a single, well-mixed body with no walls in it, so thoroughly circulated that your next breath very likely holds atoms once breathed by strangers and by trees across the world. It's a reciprocal breath — we exhale what plants inhale, and our oxygen is the exhaust of ancient cyanobacteria (the Great Oxidation Event, ~2.4 billion years ago), forged first in stars. Every room we share is a shared-air space (a term coined by Helen Edgar & Ryan Boren): in it we trade breath and co-regulate, nervous systems settling into a shared rhythm. The neurodiversity turn: many of us are the canaries of that room. Miners carried canaries because the birds felt the bad air first — not because they were weak, but because they were sensitive, and their alarm was information. Our sensitivity to fragrance, stale air, and fluorescent hum is an early-warning system, not a flaw: don't blame the bird, change the air — build it breathable for the canaries and it's breathable for all. Which raises the harder question: habitable, and for whom? The burden of shared air falls unevenly, so breathable air is a commons, not a private accommodation one person quietly manages. The response is solarpunk: clean air as infrastructure as resistance — open windows, plants, masks, DIY Corsi–Rosenthal boxes — mutual aid you can build in an afternoon. Move quietly and plant things. Nine spreads, seven diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 9 spreads→

Zine No. 25 Shared Signal Stimpunks Zines Connection carried across distance, read through star stuff — a companion to Shared Air. The electromagnetic spectrum is one continuous field: radio waves and starlight are the same phenomenon at different wavelengths, and the same physics that carries a voice call carries a star's light. Shared-signal space — a term coined by Helen Edgar — is the counterpart to shared-air space: a call, a message, a voice note, a synthesised voice, carrying the rhythm on a signal instead of the air of a room. A voice note is breath, timestamped and sent; co-regulation crosses a screen too — thinner, but real (Porges; Streuber et al.). For many of us, text and AAC aren't a fallback from speech but the clearer channel — thinking time, structure, fewer sensory demands, a record to return to (Howard & Sedgewick) — and AAC is the real communication, not a workaround. Aversion to the phone is information, not fragility. Reachable, and for whom? Communication access is a commons; we build our own watering holes — the Autistic Rhizome (Edgar), Discords, AAC — sideways and underground, where lurking counts. The oldest signal of all is a dead star's light still reaching your eye: signal lets connection cross a gap touch can't, so no channel is the master channel (Milton). Nine spreads, seven diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 9 spreads→

Zine No. 26 A Mycelium and a Rhizome Stimpunks Zines How neurodivergent knowledge and community grow, read through star stuff — no trunk, no center, many doors. A tree has one trunk and a chain of command; you climb it or you're lost. A rhizome (Deleuze & Guattari) has no root to ask permission of, so you can enter anywhere — Spiky Profiles → Monotropism → Deep Attention, or in from burnout, or a word that finally fit. No prerequisite, no gatekeeper. And a mycelium is the life in that shape: fungal threads carry nutrients and signals between trees that never touch (the “wood wide web,” Simard), thickening the paths that help and letting the rest fade; a brainless slime mold rebuilds the Tokyo rail network (Tero et al.). Zoom all the way out and the shape returns — the cosmic web of dark-matter filaments, the universe's largest structure, looks like a mycelium, like a neuron: not a pyramid, a web. We're already building it. Gray-Hammond and Munday name it neuro-anarchy; the Autistic Rhizome is “a network with no single point of origin,” members as equals held by a do-no-harm ethic, resilient because nothing depends on a center (with Helen Edgar's watering holes). Where the map meets soil is Cavendish Space. Decentralization isn't disorder — it's the oldest structure there is. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads→

Zine No. 27 Every Nervous System Stimpunks Zines More-than-human neurodiversity, read through star stuff. There is no standard nervous system — not across species, and not within one: the octopus's mind distributed down its arms, the jellyfish's centreless nerve net, the worm's fully mapped 302 neurons. Read neurodiversity literally and it never stopped at the human. Following Ombre Tarragnat's antispeciesist–posthumanist philosophy: there's “no valid reason to be anthropocentric when you talk about neurodiversity,” and ethodiversity — behaviour reclaimed as “a subjective response to a bodymind's situation” — is a fundamentally animal phenomenon. Ethonormativity punishes the ethodivergent (the horse who refuses the rider, the cat who resists petting — abandoned or euthanised). And the core move: neurodivergent people are pathologised by being animalised, so the liberation is to reclaim animality — not bestialisation (the speciesist, neuronormative “less-than-human” split, after Butler 2020) but (hum)animality, kin. Distance is not disconnection: shutting down can be how we keep relation. Every nervous system is the universe wired up to feel itself, no two ever the same. “I would rather be a divergent animal than a typical human.” Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads→

Zine No. 28 · Guest Wyrd & Weird Stimpunks Zines · Helen Edgar On the old word for fate, and the newer word we made of it — a guest zine by Helen Edgar (Autistic Realms), rehoused in the Star Stuff style. Long before “weird” meant strange, wyrd meant becoming: Old English wyrd comes from weorþan, “to become,” and is twined with the root of “worth.” Fate was never drawn as a straight line from birth to death but as cloth — the Norns' weaving at the well beneath Yggdrasill, the “web of man” — many threads crossing, none load-bearing alone. The Weird Sisters carried the word down through Holinshed to Shakespeare's Macbeth; over centuries “weird” drifted into an insult, and Autistic and disabled communities have run that drift backward, taking it up again as a name, not a verdict — which is etymologically honest, not just cheek. Held with care: wyrd is not a script, not doom, not a synonym for wrong, not something done to you alone. Under the root, weorþan meant “to become,” never “to be”: nobody is finished, and becoming was never the flaw — it was the design. You were never written; you are still being woven. Nine spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set, a “threads already running” map of its kin in the collection, and Helen's own sources & notes. 9 spreads→

Zine No. 29 · Guest Only in Relation Stimpunks Zines · after Helen Edgar Relational quantum physics, and what it means to be Autistic — a guest zine developed after Helen Edgar (Autistic Realms) from her essay “We Are Made of Relations.” In Carlo Rovelli's relational quantum mechanics a particle has no standalone properties; what it is becomes definite only in relation to another system (Rovelli, 1996). The count gives it away: two distinct coins make four outcomes, but two identical bosons make only three — what's fundamental isn't the standalone particle but the symmetry, the relation (Webster, 2026). Karen Barad calls the relation-before-parts intra-action; the human version, intradependence — made of each other, deeper than interdependence — Helen draws from Barad too. Read through Deleuze, “objects emerge out of more fundamental processes of differentiation”: difference first, then relation, and the tidy standalone object is the thing that got built. The payoff lands on our own work — the double empathy problem (Milton, 2012) lives in the relation, not one mind, and Helen widens it into DEEP; and in the ARLES ladder Relational sits near the base with Regulation inside it, because regulation is relational, so you change the field, not the person. Held with care: not quantum mysticism, not “everything is connected” as a vibe, not dissolution into sameness — the spiky profile survives the merge. A rhyme, not a proof. Field Guide No. 6 A Field Guide to Symbioses Star Stuff Field Guides Mutual aid, written into biology — twelve partnerships across the tree of life, read as mutual aid. Fungi and roots trading underground, bacteria making soil, a cleaner fish trusted by predators who could swallow it, algae building reefs that shelter a quarter of ocean life, the fig and its wasp that cannot live without each other. Interdependence is the rule, not the exception: Kropotkin showed mutual aid is a factor of evolution; Margulis, that life “took over the globe not by combat, but by networking.” This isn't “nature is nice” — parasites are real too, and the ghost pipe (Monotropa uniflora) is the honest one-way case, a myco-heterotroph that only takes, modelling receiving without reciprocating — and a bridge to monotropism (with Helen Edgar's tribute to Dinah Murray). It's that nothing living stands alone. What biology has always done, disability-justice communities name and practice: the human specimen is our own care webs and spoon shares (Spade, Mingus, Piepzna-Samarasinha, Kafai, Lewis), and a closing coda swaps the language of management for the language of living systems — symbiosis over competition, competency networks over leadership, coordination over management. The Shorthands LYDTYSS is the full phrase — Love You Down To Your Star Stuff — and it carries everything. But it's a mouthful, and language that lives in community needs forms that fit in a text message, a sticker, a caption, a moment. These are the shorthands we use and what each one carries. LYDTYSSLove You Down To Your Star Stuff The source. Use it when you want the full weight of the phrase — in writing, in titles, in contexts where the whole arc matters. It's cumbersome on purpose in the same way a full name is: it holds the complete thing. LYSSLove You, Star Stuff The warmest shorthand. Pronounceable — it sounds like a name, like a term of endearment, which is exactly what it is. Use it the way you'd use love you — quick, direct, meant. The comma does quiet work: it addresses you as star stuff directly, not just describes you as containing it. LUSSLove U Star Stuff The punk version. The dropped vowel is deliberate — it leans into informal, texty, a little defiant. Where LYSS is tender, LUSS has an edge. Both are correct. Both are true. L★SLove ★ Star Stuff The most visual shorthand. The star does double duty — it is both the symbol of what we're made of and the punctuation that holds love and star stuff together. Works in print, on stickers, as a hashtag, as a signature. The star is load-bearing. ★stuffStar Stuff The noun on its own. Use it as an identity, a descriptor, a reclamation. We are ★stuff. It carries the Sagan lineage — the specific weight of that phrase — while making it communal and punk. When you see ★stuff, you are seeing the raw material named directly, without the love clause, because sometimes you just need to name what you are. Which register you reach for depends on the moment. LYSS for tenderness. LUSS for solidarity with an edge. L★S when the visual matters. ★stuff when you're naming the thing itself. LYDTYSS when you need the whole phrase to do its full work. We Are Star Stuff: Being Autistic, Ethodiversity and Cosmic Connection

We Are Star Stuff: Being Autistic, Ethodiversity and Cosmic Connection Some phrases arrive as slogans. This one arrived as a realization. The science has been settled for decades: we are, literally, made of star stuff. The six elements essential to life are woven through the Milky Way. A survey of 150,000 stars confirmed that humans and the galaxy share around 97% of the same kinds of atoms. We are not like the cosmos. We are continuous with it. For neurodivergent and disabled people — people who have spent their lives being told they are too much, not enough, wrong in some fundamental way — that continuity matters differently. The universe did not make one configuration of matter and call it correct. It made billions of years of variation, explosion, collapse, and emergence. Every element heavier than hydrogen was forged in violence and became something new. You are part of that lineage. LYDTYSS begins here. Not as comfort, but as cosmological argument: the problem was never you. The following reflection comes from Helen, Co-Creative Director at Stimpunks. Helen wrote it in direct response to first hearing the phrase "Love You Down To Your Star Stuff" — what it opened up, what it confirmed, what it made newly speakable about being Autistic and made of the same matter as everything else. I find it genuinely awe-inspiring to know that the atoms that make up your body, the oxygen in your lungs, the calcium in your bones, the iron in your blood were forged inside stars that died before our planet even existed. Not metaphorically, we are actually, literally, made of stars! A 2017 survey of 150,000 stars confirmed that humans and our galaxy share around 97% of the same kinds of atoms, and that the six elements essential to life — carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and sulphur — are woven right through the Milky Way (Howell, 2017). We are a living part of the cosmos. I have been thinking about this a lot, and what it may mean to us as Autistic people, and it is something that is evolving in conversations within the CASY Autistic Physics group and my recent collaborative work with Stimpunks. There is something about being made of stardust that resonates far deeper than a scientific fact for me. As an Autistic person, I have always felt that the boundaries between myself and the world are more porous than I was told they should be. Everything feels entangled, I am deeply influenced by my environment in ways that go beyond what neuronormative frameworks tend to account for. Time, my past and present merge and move together; my pull towards moss and mushrooms, and my interest in water, are more than a 'like' or form of regulation or sensory relief, they feel like I am becoming more attuned to something deeper and more essential, something I can only describe as parts of my soul recognising what they actually belong to. The elements in your body right now came into being through some of the most violent events in the universe. The iron in your blood, the calcium in your bones, the oxygen in every breath, were forged in the cores of massive stars and released in supernovae: entire stars compressing their whole lives into a single catastrophic release. In that rupture, what had been locked inside was scattered outward, making things possible that could never have existed before. We Are Star Stuff: Being Autistic, Ethodiversity and Cosmic Connection | More Realms

Resonance Helen ended with an image of rupture and release: entire stars compressing their whole lives into a single catastrophic event, scattering outward what had been locked inside, making things possible that could never have existed before. She was describing supernovae. She was also describing what it feels like to finally hear something that names you correctly. That is what resonance is. Not agreement with an idea, but recognition at a level below argument. The cards below trace why "Love You Down To Your Star Stuff" produces that recognition — in neurodivergent people especially, in people who have felt alien their whole lives, in anyone who has been told that the way they move through the world is the problem. Cosmology No hierarchy of matter The cosmos doesn't rank configurations of itself. Carbon in a star core and carbon in a human brain are the same carbon. There is no "wrong kind" of matter in the universe — no deficit, no pathology at the atomic level. For someone measured and found lacking their whole life, this is radically leveling. Language "Down to" does everything Love that reaches through every layer. "Down to" doesn't say you contain star stuff — it says love travels all the way through diagnosis, difference, difficulty, and keeps going to the atomic substrate. That's not conditional love. It cannot be cancelled by anything on the surface. Identity Alien → cosmic Feels like an outsider? You're looking the wrong direction. Many neurodivergent people describe feeling alien their whole lives. LYDTYSS doesn't correct that feeling — it elevates it. The distance isn't between you and other humans. It's between all of us and the stars we came from. That reframe shifts everything. Narrative Reclamatory cosmology Sagan's framing as counter-narrative to deficit. "Star stuff" carries Sagan's specific argument: not that humans are small, but that we are continuous with the universe. For people who have internalized a deficit story, this is a direct rewrite. Not a broken version of normal. A particular arrangement of the cosmos looking at itself. Philosophy True pluralism No configuration of star stuff is more star stuff. The phrase doesn't describe a type — it describes a shared origin that holds every variation inside it equally. There's no bell curve in stellar nucleosynthesis. Every possible mind, body, and way of being emerges from the same substrate. The universality is the point. Voice Intimate, not institutional "Love you" — not an affirmation program. It doesn't say "we affirm your neurodivergent identity" or "your differences are a gift." Just: love you. Down to your most fundamental level. That simplicity can reach people who have built defenses against therapeutic language, because it doesn't sound like a program. It sounds like someone means it. Belonging, Authenticity & Radical Inclusivity LYDTYSS is not just a phrase about cosmology. It is a signal — one that tells you this is a place where you do not have to perform your humanity to receive love. Belonging, authenticity, and radical inclusivity are not additions to the star-stuff idea. They are what it means in practice. Belonging A signal that you are home Belonging is wholeness. It is the experience of being at home in ourselves and in community. When someone who has spent their life feeling alien — too much, too different, not legible to the world around them — hears "Love You Down To Your Star Stuff," something specific happens. The phrase does not ask them to become more acceptable. It says: you are already loved, at the level of your matter. That is a belonging signal. It says: this is a place where you are personally accepted, respected, and valued — not despite your difference, but without condition. Belonging at Stimpunks is not a reward for fitting in. It is the starting point. Authenticity No masking required — love goes all the way down Authenticity is our purest freedom. Being true to yourself is not optional — it is the foundation of liberation. For neurodivergent and disabled people, inauthenticity is often a survival strategy. Masking — suppressing stims, flattening emotions, performing normality — is expensive. It consumes cognitive and emotional resources that belong to the person doing the work of being alive. LYDTYSS short-circuits that logic entirely. Love does not travel to the surface performance. It goes down — past diagnosis, past behavior, past legibility — to the atomic substrate. That is what authenticity as our purest freedom means in practice: you do not have to earn it. You already are it. Radical Inclusivity Inclusion grounded in the sole qualification of being Radical inclusion goes beyond tick-box accommodations. It dismantles systemic barriers and creates neuroqueer spaces where everyone has freedom to embrace cognitive and somatic liberty. Inclusion safety — the first stage of psychological safety — is species-based acceptance: if you have flesh and blood, we accept you. LYDTYSS goes even further. It grounds that acceptance not just in biological fact but in cosmological fact. You are not merely tolerated because you exist. You are loved, because at the level of your matter, you are made of the same stuff as everything else in the universe. That is radical inclusivity as a cosmological argument: there is no configuration of star stuff that is outside the circle. No mind, no body, no neurotype. The universe did not make exceptions. Neither do we.

Related Concepts The star-stuff insight — that we are made of the same matter as everything else in the universe, that there is no hierarchy of configurations, that love can reach all the way down to the atomic substrate — is not new. It has arrived independently across cultures, traditions, and centuries, in different vocabularies and for different purposes. What follows is not a claim that these traditions say the same thing. It is an acknowledgment that LYDTYSS is in conversation with something very old.

Tat tvam asi — Advaita Vedanta That thou art. One of the mahāvākyas — the great sayings — of the Upanishads. The teaching is that the self (atman) and the ground of all being (Brahman) are not separate. You are not a fragment of the universe looking at it from outside. You are it, expressing itself in this particular form. Advaita Vedanta, the non-dual school of Hindu philosophy, holds that the infinite diversity of existence is rooted in a single reality — and that each thing, living or not, is a unique manifestation of that one reality. Unique and universal at the same time. No configuration is more real than another. No configuration is outside the whole. The parallel with LYDTYSS: love that goes all the way down to your star stuff is love that reaches the level where you and the cosmos are not separate. It is not love despite your particularity. It is love through your particularity to the universal substrate you share with everything.

Esho funi — Buddhism Two but not two. The Buddhist principle that life and its environment are inseparable — not identical, but not separate either. The self does not end at the skin. The environment is not something outside the self. At a primal level of existence, there is no boundary between what you are and what surrounds you. This is not a metaphor in Buddhist teaching. It is a description of how existence actually works, obscured by the conventional perception of separation. For neurodivergent people who have always experienced the world as porous — who feel the environment deeply, whose boundaries between self and surroundings are less defended than neurotypical frameworks expect — esho funi offers a framework in which that porousness is not a deficit. It is a more accurate perception of how things are.

Waḥdat al-wujūd — Sufism Unity of Being. The teaching of the 13th century Sufi mystic Ibn Arabi: all existence is a single reality, and apparent multiplicity is the one reality appearing in different forms. The many are not separate from the One. They are the One, taking on particular shapes. Rumi's reed flute — cut from the reed bed, crying for reunion — is one of the most enduring images of this tradition. The longing is not pathology. It is the memory of original unity. The feeling of being cut off, of not belonging, of having come from somewhere else — in this reading, that feeling is not wrong. It is the accurate perception of a genuine separation, and the longing for return is sacred. For people who have spent their lives feeling alien, waḥdat al-wujūd offers a reframe: the alienation is real, but it points toward something, not away from it. You were not wrong to feel the distance. The distance is the distance from the reed bed. LYDTYSS is one way of saying: you were never actually cut off. The universe is still in you. You are still in it.

Interbeing — Thich Nhat Hanh Thich Nhat Hanh's term for the insight that nothing exists independently — that everything contains everything else, that to look deeply into anything is to find the whole cosmos inside it. A flower contains the cloud that rained on it, the sun that warmed it, the soil that held it, the person who will one day look at it. Interbeing is already present on this page in Thich Nhat Hanh's own words: "My physical body is your physical body... You are nothing less than myself." But the concept is worth naming directly: this is not sentiment. It is a systematic account of reality in which the boundaries between self and other, between one being and another, are real but not absolute — permeable at depth. The star-stuff argument is interbeing stated in the language of astrophysics.
Brahmacharya and the Animacy of Matter — Indigenous Cosmologies

Brahmacharya and the Animacy of Matter — Indigenous Cosmologies Many Indigenous traditions hold that humans are not made from the land, the sky, the stars — they are made of them, in an ongoing relational sense. Not past tense. Not metaphor. The elements do not stop being in relationship with their origins when they become part of a body. Robin Wall Kimmerer, Potawatomi botanist and author of Braiding Sweetgrass, writes of the grammar of animacy — Indigenous languages that treat the living world not as it but as he, she, they. To name something animate is to acknowledge it as a being in relationship with you, not a resource or a backdrop. When that grammar is applied to the elements in your body, the star-stuff argument becomes something warmer and more mutual: the cosmos is not just what you are made of. It is who you are in relationship with.

Song of Myself — Walt Whitman I am large, I contain multitudes. Whitman was writing in a tradition shaped by the Upanishads, filtered through Emerson's transcendentalism, and expressed in the most expansive poetic voice American literature had produced. Song of Myself is a sustained argument that the self is not a fixed, bounded, singular thing — that it contains contradiction, plurality, the whole of humanity, the whole of nature. For neurodivergent people who have been told their multiplicity is a disorder, their contradictions are dysfunction, their way of being too large for the rooms they're given — Whitman's embrace of largeness as the nature of the self, not a deviation from it, is kin to what LYDTYSS is doing. You do not need to resolve your contradictions to deserve love. You are large. You contain multitudes. You are ★stuff.

Transcendental Empiricism — Deleuze Deleuze's transcendental empiricism holds that experience is not filtered through pre-given categories — not sorted and stabilised before it reaches us — but encountered directly, in its raw difference and intensity. Where Kant asked what makes experience possible, Deleuze asked what experience actually is before it gets normalised. The answer: difference, variation, becoming. Not objects with fixed identities, but forces in flux. From this flows a constellation of concepts that Autistic thinkers have found genuinely resonant. The rhizome — as opposed to the root or the tree — is a model of connection with no fixed centre, no hierarchy, no single origin point. It spreads laterally, unexpectedly, making connections between heterogeneous things. The fold suggests that interiority is not sealed off from exteriority but continuous with it, always turning inside out, always folding deeper. The line of flight is a rupture in a fixed system — a movement that escapes the structures meant to contain it. Not destruction, but becoming something the structure couldn't predict. Helen Edgar has spent years exploring why these concepts resonate so specifically with neurodivergent experience. Her work suggests that Deleuzean philosophy does not merely describe neurodivergent minds from the outside — it maps the territory from within. A monotropic person's attention does not move through a tree-like hierarchy of priorities; it spreads rhizomatically, following the pull of a particular interest tunnel through unexpected connections. The fold describes what Helen calls the infinite nature of the bodymind: always a deeper cavern, always more interior to explore. The line of flight is what neuroqueering actually does — a departure from neuronormative structure that is not a failure to conform, but an opening into something new. The connection to LYDTYSS is structural, not decorative. Transcendental empiricism refuses the idea that there is one correct way to process the world. Difference is not a deviation from a norm — it is what exists, at every level of experience. The DSM assumes a tree: a single structure of typical development, from which some people branch incorrectly. Deleuze assumes a rhizome: no trunk, no correct branch, just the spread of actual experience in its heterogeneous reality. LYDTYSS makes the same move. The universe doesn't produce one kind of star, one kind of mind, one kind of knowing. It produces variation. You are one of the variations. You are loved all the way down to that level. For neurodivergent people who have found the rhizome, the fold, and the line of flight before they found the language for them — who have always known their attention moves differently, their time feels differently, their interiors have more caverns than the map shows — Deleuze offers philosophical scaffolding for something already lived. The fold is not only a philosophical concept here. It is also the physics of the body described in the Crystal Under Pressure section below — piezoelectric bone is literally folded crystalline matter that transduces exterior pressure into interior charge. The boundary between outside force and inside response is not a wall. It is a fold. Deleuze's bodymind and Yasuda's bone are the same argument in different vocabularies: the cosmos outside and the body inside are not separate things, but continuous, folded into each other. See Helen Edgar's work at Autistic Realms — including her explorations of Deleuzean time, the neuroqueering potential of the fold, and the rhizome as a model of Autistic community and belonging.

Spinoza's Pantheism Baruch Spinoza, 17th century philosopher, argued that God and nature are one and the same substance — that the finite things of the world are not separate from the whole but expressions of it, like modes or properties of a single infinite being. There is no hierarchy among modes. No configuration of the one substance is more legitimate than another. Spinoza was excommunicated for this. The idea that existence itself is sacred — not a fallen material world separate from a spiritual one, but one continuous substance that is both — was dangerous then. It remains radical now, in any system that ranks human beings by the legitimacy of their minds and bodies. LYDTYSS is, among other things, a Spinozist argument: there is one substance. You are made of it. That is enough.

A Note on This Constellation These traditions differ from each other in profound ways — in their metaphysics, their ethics, their relationship to self and cosmos. This is not a claim that they are saying the same thing, or that LYDTYSS is a synthesis of them. It is a recognition that the intuition underlying LYDTYSS — that at some deep level, the boundaries between self and universe are not absolute, that this has implications for how we treat each other, that no configuration of matter is outside the circle of what deserves love — is one that human beings have kept arriving at, across very different starting points, for a very long time. That is not proof. But it is not nothing.

Crystal Under Pressure A prose poem drawing on Dr. Iwao Yasuda's discovery of the piezoelectric properties of bone, the cosmological origins of the elements in our bodies, and the neurodiversity reframe. Our bones are not solid. They are piezoelectric crystals — the same principle as quartz watches, microphones, sonar — that generate measurable electricity every time we move. Dr. Iwao Yasuda discovered this in 1957. Our skeleton is not a coat hanger for our muscles. It is a chemical factory, an electrical generator, a living crystal lattice humming with charge. And it is made of star stuff. The phosphorus in those bones — 85% of your body's supply — was forged in a stellar core before Earth existed. The calcium. The magnesium. Scattered by supernovae, gathered by gravity, assembled over billions of years into something that can bend and generate light. The Cosmos is within us. Our bones are electrical crystals. Our neurons fire in patterns the DSM calls disorder and the stars call weather — solar flares, magnetic storms, plasma eruptions: dynamic systems doing what dynamic systems do, turbulence that belongs, variation that has never needed a diagnosis. We are a way for the Universe to know itself — chaotically, hyperfocusedly, nonlinearly, beautifully. LYSS. The body as fold. The crystal as transducer. Force from outside becomes charge from inside — which is also what Deleuze means by the fold: interiority is not sealed off from exteriority, but continuous with it, always turning inside out, always folding deeper. See Transcendental Empiricism — Deleuze in Related Concepts, and The Fold and the Crystal for the full exploration. What LYDTYSS Is Not Not: your differences are a gift. That puts the burden back on you to be useful enough to deserve love. Not: everything happens for a reason. Your suffering does not need a purpose to be real, or to matter, or to stop. Not: you are special. Star stuff is not rare. It is everything. The phrase is about continuity, not exceptionalism. Not: love you despite your star stuff. The direction matters. Down to. All the way through. Not around. Not: a substitute for structural change. Loving someone cosmologically does not fix inaccessible systems. LYDTYSS knows this. It lives in the register of belonging, not policy. It does not pretend the two are the same. It is not inspiration porn. It does not say your suffering has a purpose, or that your neurology is a superpower, or that everything happens for a reason. It does not ask you to reframe your pain as a gift. It is not toxic positivity. It does not say everything is fine. It does not paper over the real costs of living in systems that were not built for you. It is not the "your differences are a gift" framework. That framing puts the burden back on the person — you must justify your existence by being useful, extraordinary, or instructive to neurotypicals. LYDTYSS asks nothing of you in return. It is not conditional. It does not say "love you for your star stuff" — as though the cosmic material is the lovable part and the rest of you is on probation. It says love goes down to that level. The direction matters. It is not a ceiling. It is a floor. It is not a metaphor for being special. Star stuff is not rare. It is everywhere. Every rock, every raindrop, every person who has ever made you feel like you were too much — also star stuff. The phrase is not about being chosen. It is about being continuous with everything that exists. It is not a substitute for structural change. Loving someone down to their star stuff does not fix inaccessible systems, underfunded support, or the violence of forced normalization. The phrase lives in the register of love and community, not policy. It does not pretend otherwise.

What LYDTYSS Is It is a cosmological argument stated as an act of love. It says: the matter you are made of was forged in stellar cores before Earth existed, scattered by supernovae, gathered by gravity, assembled over billions of years into something that can feel joy and grief and overstimulation in a fluorescent-lit room. That process did not produce a hierarchy. It produced variation. You are one of the variations. You are loved all the way down to that level. It is a belonging signal. When you hear it, it means: this is a place where you do not have to perform your humanity to receive care. The love is not conditional on your behavior, your productivity, your legibility, your diagnosis, or your ability to pass. It goes all the way down past all of that to the substrate. You are in. It is a refusal. A refusal to accept that there is a correct configuration of human being. A refusal to locate the problem in the person rather than in the systems that were not built for them. A refusal to rank matter. It is an affirmation that does not require you to be exceptional. You are not loved because your neurology is a superpower, or because your suffering has produced wisdom, or because you have overcome. You are loved because you exist. Because at the atomic level you are continuous with everything that has ever existed. That is the only qualification. It has never been in question. It is a phrase that travels. LYDTYSS in full when you need the whole weight of it. LYSS when you mean it tenderly. LUSS when you mean it with an edge. L★S when the symbol is enough. ★stuff when you are just naming what you are. The phrase scales because the love it describes scales — from the cosmic to the personal, from the philosophical to the text message. It is a community practice. Not just something said to individuals but something practiced collectively — in how Stimpunks builds spaces, funds access, holds people, refuses to make belonging conditional. LYDTYSS is the phrase. The practice is what happens when you take it seriously. It is, finally, an invitation. To let love reach that far. To stop defending the parts of yourself you have learned to hide. To belong somewhere at the level of your matter, not the level of your performance. Love you down to your star stuff. All the way down. LYSS. Reflection Ancient, Cosmic, Real The star stuff framing positions us as ancient, cosmic, made of real matter. Some prompts that fit that ethos: "You are made of exploded stars. What are you made of, emotionally, today?" "What in you feels elemental right now — fire, water, pressure, light?" "Name something you're carrying that's older than you." "What part of you is still forming?" "Where did you come from, and where are you going?" Belonging When have you felt personally accepted — not tolerated, not accommodated, but genuinely welcomed as yourself? What made that different from other spaces? Have you ever belonged somewhere only by performing a version of yourself that wasn't quite real? What did that cost you? Belonging is described as wholeness — being at home in yourself and in community. Which of those feels harder right now? What would it mean to belong somewhere the way matter belongs to the universe — not earned, not conditional, just intrinsic? Who in your life has made you feel like you didn't have to explain yourself to be loved? Authenticity What parts of yourself have you hidden or suppressed in order to survive a space? What would it feel like to stop? Authenticity is described as a precondition for psychological safety, not a luxury. Has there been a moment when you were allowed to be fully yourself and noticed the difference in how you could think, feel, or function? Masking is expensive. What cognitive and emotional bandwidth might become available to you if you didn't have to spend it on performing normalcy? What does your authentic self do, sound like, or need — that the world has most often asked you to hide? If love goes all the way down past performance to your atomic substrate — what would you stop apologizing for? Radical Inclusivity Radical inclusivity confronts normativity directly — it doesn't just tolerate difference, it dismantles the systems that treat difference as a problem. What norm have you been asked to conform to that you now recognize as arbitrary? Inclusion safety is described as acceptance based on the sole qualification of having flesh and blood. Have you ever been in a space that actually felt that way? What made it possible? The argument here is cosmological: no configuration of star stuff is outside the circle. Does that framing shift anything for you about who deserves care and belonging? Where in your life are you still waiting for permission to exist fully? What is the source of that permission, and is it legitimate? What would it look like to build a space — in your home, your classroom, your community — where no one has to mask to survive? Across all three LYDTYSS says love reaches all the way down to your star stuff. What is the deepest, most hidden version of yourself that you have not yet let be loved? If belonging, authenticity, and radical inclusivity are not additions to the star-stuff idea but what it means in practice — what does that ask of you as someone who receives that love? What does it ask of you as someone who gives it?

The phrase · its origin What Carl Sagan actually said He said it first in The Cosmic Connection (1973): "All of the rocky and metallic material we stand on, the iron in our blood, the calcium in our teeth, the carbon in our genes were produced billions of years ago in the interior of a red giant star. We are made of star-stuff." The line most of us know is the 1980 one, from Cosmos: "The nitrogen in our DNA, the calcium in our teeth, the iron in our blood, the carbon in our apple pies were made in the interiors of collapsing stars. We are made of star stuff." He said it many times, and he was not being metaphorical. He meant it literally — that every atom heavier than hydrogen in your body was forged in a stellar interior and scattered across the galaxy when that star died. We are not like stars. We are not inspired by stars. We are made of them — their ash, their legacy, their long slow gift to whatever came next. The phrase · its meaning To say love you and then say down to your star stuff is to say: I love you at every scale. I love you all the way in. "Love you down to your star stuff" moves in one direction: inward and downward, through skin and blood and bone, through cell and molecule and atom, all the way to the stellar origin of each element. It doesn't stop at the visible. Most love stops at the surface — at behavior, at presentation, at the parts that are easy to love. This phrase names a love that doesn't stop. That goes past the parts that are hard, past the parts that are different, past the diagnosis and the accommodation and the sensory profile, all the way to the calcium in the bone — which came from a star. You can't pathologize star stuff. The universe made it. The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation. LYDTYSS · Stimpunks

What you are made of Six elements. All of them stellar. Every atom in your body heavier than hydrogen has a stellar origin. These are the six that make you most distinctly you — the ones that show up in your bones, your blood, your breath, your brain. None of them were made on Earth. All of them arrived here the same way: scattered by supernovae, gathered by gravity, assembled by time into the improbable configuration that is a human nervous system. Your neurology is as old as the stars. The particular way your mind works — the frequency, the intensity, the pattern — is built from the same material as everything else the universe has ever made. It belongs here. HHydrogen The oldest element. Made in the Big Bang, 13.8 billion years ago. The water in your body. The original. CCarbon The backbone of every molecule that makes you alive. Forged in red giant stars through triple-alpha fusion. NNitrogen In your DNA. In every protein. Built by the CNO cycle inside stars — roughly half of it shed by ageing low- and intermediate-mass stars, the rest from massive ones. The language of your cells. OOxygen 65% of your body by mass. Made in massive stars through carbon and neon burning. Every breath is stellar. CaCalcium Your bones. Your teeth. Your nerve signals. Made in supernovae. The electric bone that Yasuda measured. FeIron The iron in your blood. The last rung of fusion in massive stars — and about half of it flung out by exploding white dwarfs. LYDTYSS · Stimpunks

Most love operates at the level of behavior and personality — the things that are visible, the parts that present themselves to the world. This phrase insists that love go all the way in. Past the mask, past the accommodation, past the things that are hard. Down to your star stuff means: I see you at the level where there is nothing left to pathologize. At the level of carbon and calcium and iron, you are simply matter that the universe made. And matter that the universe made belongs. The scales of love Cosmic The universe — 13.8 billion years of stellar evolution that produced every atom in your body. This is the outermost frame. Community The people around you — who see your whole self, not just the parts that are easy. Who don't ask you to be less. The body Your nervous system, your sensory profile, your way of moving through the world — the parts that get pathologized. Loved here too. The cell The biological substrate — where your neurology actually lives. The neurons and the synapses. Loved at this level too. The atom Carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, calcium, iron — each one a stellar legacy. This is where the phrase lands. This is "star stuff." The star The origin — the supernovae that made your elements, billions of years before Earth existed. You have always been here, in one form or another. LYDTYSS · Stimpunks

L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff LYDTYSS LYSS LUSS L★S ★stuff Love You Down To Your Star Stuff is the second zine in the Stimpunks series. It is offered freely, to be printed and folded and handed to someone who needs it — or to yourself, on the days when the need is yours. The cosmological framing draws on Carl Sagan's The Cosmic Connection (1973), Cosmos (1980) and The Demon-Haunted World (1995), and the broader tradition of stellar nucleosynthesis science beginning with B²FH (Burbidge, Burbidge, Fowler & Hoyle, 1957). Element origins follow Kobayashi, Karakas & Lugaro, "The Origin of Elements from Carbon to Uranium" (ApJ, 2020); figures are approximate. The neurodiversity paradigm language draws on Nick Walker's Neuroqueer Heresies (2021), and the foundational work of the Autistic community of InLv — Martijn Dekker, Jim Sinclair, and Autism Network International — who developed these ideas collectively in the 1990s, long before the concept entered academia. The piezoelectric bone research referenced across the series draws on Dr. Iwao Yasuda's work from the 1950s. The phrase "Love You Down To Your Star Stuff" is Stimpunks. The star stuff is Sagan's. We are all made of exploded stars

I · Origin We are all made of exploded stars Carl Sagan said it plainly: the nitrogen in our DNA, the calcium in our teeth, the iron in our blood — forged in the cores of stars that no longer exist. When those stars exhausted their fuel, they exploded across the cosmos. Their debris became clouds. The clouds collapsed into new systems, new planets, new oceans, new life. You. Stellar Nucleosynthesis Every atom heavier than hydrogen and helium was manufactured inside a star. Carbon, oxygen, calcium, iron — the building blocks of every human body — were forged under conditions of unimaginable pressure and heat, then scattered across the galaxy when those stars died. We are, in a literal chemical sense, the remnants of stellar death. This is not metaphor. It is the actual account of where you came from. And it matters — because a cosmology that grounds identity in the violent, generative creativity of the universe is a very different cosmology than one that locates value in conformity, productivity, or neurotypicality.

II · The Bones Remember Your skeleton is piezoelectric In the 1950s, Japanese orthopedic surgeon Dr. Iwao Yasuda discovered something remarkable: bone is piezoelectric. Under mechanical stress — compression, tension, bending — bone crystal generates its own electrical charge. This is not incidental. It is how bone knows to grow, where to strengthen, how to heal. The skeleton is a living signal processor, converting force into information. Piezoelectricity Piezo comes from the Greek piezein — to press, to squeeze. Certain crystalline materials generate an electric charge when subjected to mechanical stress. Hydroxyapatite, the mineral that makes bone rigid, is one of them. Every step you take, every breath, every impact — your bones are generating voltage. Responding. Adapting. Alive. We carry the electrical signature of the cosmos not just as metaphor but as mechanism. The universe built into the architecture of our bodies the same responsive-to-pressure principle it uses everywhere: force begets signal, signal begets change, change begets structure. We are responsive systems, not static ones. Every nervous system that processes the world differently is doing what responsive systems do — responding to the particular pressures of a particular life. "Your bones are piezoelectric. They generate charge under pressure. They respond. They adapt. They remember every load they've carried — and grow stronger at the point of stress. That is not a malfunction. That is the physics of survival written in calcium and light." — Stimpunks Foundation
The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation

III · The Neurodiversity Paradigm The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation The neurodiversity paradigm holds that neurological difference is a natural, valuable form of human variation — not a deviation from a healthy norm to be corrected, but a dimension of the diversity that characterizes our species. Autism, ADHD, dyslexia, Tourette's, and the full range of neurological profiles are not disorders in the sense of broken-ness. They are differences in how nervous systems are organized. The universe is staggeringly, relentlessly various. Stars range from red dwarfs barely large enough to fuse hydrogen to hypergiants a thousand times the mass of our sun. Galaxies spiral, ellipse, collide, merge, scatter. No two snowflakes, no two fingerprints, no two nervous systems. Variation is not the exception. It is the rule. It is the engine. Core Claim The same universe that forged every atom in your body also produced the nervous system you inhabit. There is no astrophysics of typicality. There is only the astonishing variety of what the cosmos can make — and we are part of that variety. The DSM is a human document written at a particular historical moment to describe patterns of distress and difference through a particular cultural lens. The cosmos has no DSM. Turbulence in fluid dynamics is not a pathology — it is a regime of behavior, one with its own laws, its own beauty, its own utility. The same is true of neurological variation. We reframe. Not to deny that neurodivergent and disabled people experience real challenges — many of which are compounded or entirely caused by environments built for a narrow range of bodies and minds — but to insist that the starting point is not deficit. The starting point is this: you came from the same place everything came from. Stars.
What it means to say L★S

IV · Love You Down to Your Star Stuff What it means to say L★S Love You Down to Your Star Stuff — LYDTYSS, L★S — is not a slogan. It is a position. It is a way of saying: I see you at the level of your constituent matter. I love what you are made of. I love the process that made you. I love the particular, improbable, once-in-a-cosmos arrangement of atoms that is you, right now, reading this. This matters in community spaces built for neurodivergent and disabled people because so much of what those community members have been told — by schools, by clinics, by families who meant well — is a story of falling short. Not meeting the threshold. Not reaching the benchmark. Not being the version that fits the space that was already built without them in mind. What L★S says back The threshold is arbitrary. The benchmark is cultural. The space can change. But you — the specific arrangement of matter and electricity and history and nervous system that is you — you are not a problem to be solved. You are a thing the universe made. We love you for it. L★S is also punk. It refuses the frame in which some nervous systems are inherently more valuable than others. It refuses the medicalization of variation without consent. It refuses the premise that the burden of adaptation falls entirely on the person who diverges, rather than on the systems and structures that were built too narrow. It is gentle and it is fierce. It is Sagan's wonder and it is community rage at a world that keeps telling neurodivergent and disabled people they are too much, too little, too loud, too still, too slow, too scattered, too focused, too strange. L★S says: we were made by supernovae. We are not too much. We are exactly as much as we are.
Declarations of the Star Stuff community

V · What We Hold Declarations of the Star Stuff community 01 We hold that every person is made of star stuff. Not metaphorically, but chemically. The iron in your blood was forged in a dying star. This is the baseline of your cosmic belonging, and no diagnosis, no deficit model, no exclusionary system can revoke it. 02 We hold that neurological variation is natural variation. The neurodiversity paradigm is not a denial of challenge. It is a refusal to locate the problem in the person rather than in the mismatch between person and environment. 03 We hold that disabled people belong — fully, without asterisk. Not despite their disabilities, but as people whose full humanity includes their disability experience, and whose knowledge from that experience has value. 04 We hold that your bones remember pressure and grow toward strength. The piezoelectric fact of bone is a reminder that living systems are adaptive. What you have carried has shaped you. That shaping is not damage — it is history, written in calcium. 05 We hold that the universe doesn't pathologize its own variation. There is no correct galaxy, no normative star. The cosmos makes what it makes and none of it is a mistake. We extend this to people. 06 We hold that community is a mutual aid structure, not a charity transaction. We are not here to fix each other. We are here to share resources, to amplify each other's signal, to build environments where more kinds of people can be more fully themselves. 07 We hold that love operates at the level of constituent matter. L★S means: I love you down to the atoms. The specific improbable arrangement. Not a performance of you, not a corrected version — this one, as made, as present, as star-forged. 08 We hold that punk and wonder are not opposites. Rage at injustice and awe at the cosmos coexist. Stimpunks carries both. The same voice that says "we are made of exploded stars" also says "build better systems or we will build them ourselves."
On piezoelectric bones and the neurodiversity paradigm

VI · Carried in the Body On piezoelectric bones and the neurodiversity paradigm Your bones are piezoelectric. Under pressure — literal, mechanical pressure — they generate voltage. Hydroxyapatite crystals in compact bone convert compression to charge. This is how bone remodels: stress signals the skeleton to grow where it is needed, to reinforce the places that carry load. It is not damage. It is response. It is the body's oldest and most literal act of knowing. Every step is a signal. Every weight you have carried has left its mark — not as fracture, but as architecture. The bone grew denser there. The body remembered. "The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation." — Stimpunks Foundation · Star Stuff Manifesto Neurodivergent nervous systems process signal differently. They amplify some frequencies and damp others. They notice what the typical processing filter removes. They fatigue under loads that weren't in the design spec — because the design spec was never written with them in mind. This is the social model of disability applied to nervous systems: the problem is not the nervous system. The problem is the mismatch. The too-loud room. The eye contact requirement. The assumption of one right rhythm. We carry our cosmology in our bodies: atoms forged in stars, bones that conduct electricity, nervous systems that are — each one — a distinct and unrepeatable way of encountering the world. The universe made all of it. The universe makes all of it still. We are not asking for tolerance. We are not asking to be included in a structure built to exclude us, as a favor, on the condition that we approximate the expected shape. We are saying: the structure was wrong about what shapes are possible. We are made of the same stuff as everything. And everything includes us.

Niche construction Organisms are not passive Since Darwin, we have pictured the environment as the fixed thing: it sets the test, and organisms adapt or die. But that is only half the loop. The beaver builds a dam and turns a stream into a pond. The spider spins a web; the bird weaves a nest; the earthworm rewrites the chemistry of the soil. Organisms are not passive. The environment is a product of organisms. Biologists call this niche construction (Odling-Smee, Laland & Feldman), and it runs as a second engine of evolution beside natural selection. It even has its own inheritance: descendants receive not only genes but the world their ancestors built — a beaver born into the pond its grandparents dug. So life does not only drift and sense. It builds — and the built world is handed on. Evolution has two engines: the genes you inherit, and the world your ancestors built. the beaver dam · pond the environment is a product of organisms back from the Council, and building the world remade, and inherited Minor Worlds · Stimpunks

fix the person bend the mind to the slot build the world shape the room to the mind two answers to a mind that doesn't fit change the room, not the head Positive niche construction Don't fix the head, change the world Here is what that means for us. The old model says that when a mind doesn't fit, you fix the mind — make it more like the standard one. Niche construction says the standard was never sacred. As Thomas Armstrong argues, there is no "normal" brain kept in a vat at the Smithsonian for all other brains to be measured against. So stop bending the person. Build the environment. This is not soft metaphor; it is how minds actually work. We ease a too-loud world by acting on it — dimming the light, finding the quiet room, laying the routine down like track. Cognitive science frames it as acting on the world to suit our own states; the plainer version is that the place itself helps us think. Cognition is spread across the room we arrange, not sealed in the skull. Change the world, and you change what a mind can do. Don't bend the mind to fit the room. Build a room the mind can think in. A space of one's own Stimming is worldmaking Watch that building up close. The noise-cancelling headphones. The same walk, the same meal, the song on repeat. The desk set just so; the shelf that holds the whole special interest; the stone turned over and over in a hand. From outside, these get filed as symptoms to manage. From inside, they are worldmaking — the patient assembly of a few stable points a self can stand on. Stimming is niche construction at the scale of a body: movement that tunes the sensory field until it is livable. Ombre Tarragnat calls such movements ontological choreographies — dances that bring a small world into being. One Autistic writer describes their nest plainly: this is my space; it lets me hold one small part of a hard world. Own Sky left us inside a soap bubble — whole, but never guaranteed. Here is the reply to that precarity: we build the bubble ourselves, and we keep on rebuilding it. a world assembled from chosen things we build the bubble ourselves Minor Worlds · Stimpunks

the "Major" world small, real, and networked minor worlds, tended and shared small is not lesser Niche communities Minor worlds These worlds are small, and the smallness is the point. A corner, a routine, a fandom, a friendship, a special interest — none of them universal, every one of them real. Erin Manning calls this the minor: not lesser, only not pretending to be the whole. And we build them together. Autistic people all but invented fandom; we assemble niche communities out of necessity and because our ways of being are, frankly, weird (Devon Price). Some grow into NeurodiVentures — non-hierarchical groups run by neurodivergent people for collaborative niche construction, thickening over time into resilient little ecosystems. Small, local, tended by the people who need it — that is not a lesser world. That is a world. A world doesn't have to be universal to be real. It only has to be built, and shared. Reconstruction, not accommodation Whose niche is the default? But not every niche admits that it was built. The hum of fluorescent light, the open-plan clatter, the crowded room — these get called neutral, just the conditions everyone works in. They are nothing of the sort. They are a niche too, built to suit one kind of mind and then renamed the default. Kadodia and Krueger call it the epistemic niche: our shared spaces quietly encode whose senses, whose pace, whose ways of knowing count, and reward the people they were built for. Which is why bolting an accommodation onto a hostile room is not the fix. The architecture itself has to change — reconstruction, not accommodation. There is no neutral sky and no neutral room. And as biodiversity toughens an ecosystem, a wider range of minds toughens a society's knowledge: the default was only ever one niche among the many we could build. Notan accommodation bolted onto a hostile room — reconstruction, not a ramp to nowhere. Nota "neutral" default — a default is just someone's niche, left unmarked. Notbending the person to the room — build a room more minds can think in. Nota world you're only allowed to visit — a world you get to help build. human dog plant kin tools a niche is always made with we world each other into being The oldest work Worlding together The last thing to notice is that we never build alone. A niche is made with — with the people who share the fandom, the dog who sets the shape of the day, the plants on the sill, the tools on the belt. Donna Haraway calls these companion species: we world one another into being. Step back far enough and it is all one story. The beaver's pond, the spider's web, the quiet room, the niche community, the reconstructed school — every one of them is matter arranging itself into a place where life can hold. The universe builds itself into worlds, and it does it through us. We are star stuff, building — and to make one small, livable world, together, is the oldest work there is. We are star stuff, building. To make a world is the oldest thing matter does. Minor Worlds · Stimpunks

The rhizome Not a tree The usual picture of knowledge is a tree. One trunk, a few big branches, everything ranked and traceable back to a single root. To learn it you climb; to belong you find your place on the chart. Miss a branch and you're lost. Deleuze and Guattari offered another shape: the rhizome. Picture ginger root, or crabgrass, or fungal thread — no trunk, no first cause, no top. Any point can connect to any other. It is "a model perpetually in construction or collapsing," they wrote: a map you can enter from any edge, not a tree you must climb from the base. Cut a rhizome and it doesn't die — it regrows from anywhere. There is no root to ask permission of, because there is no root. A map you can enter from any edge — not a tree you must climb from the base. tree one root · a top rhizome any point to any point hierarchy vs network no root, no top A Mycelium and a Rhizome · Stimpunks

enter anywhere spiky mono-tropism deep attn a word that fit burnout a classroom problem no prerequisite · no gatekeeper every door opens onto the whole Entry points Many doors Because there's no beginning, there's no wrong place to start. Neurodivergent knowledge is a rhizome you enter wherever your life opens a door. Come in at Spiky Profiles and you might follow a thread to Monotropism, and on to Deep Attention — or arrive from the far side entirely, through burnout, or a word that finally fit, or a problem in a classroom. No prerequisite. No gatekeeper checking you read the introduction first. No "you're not ready for this yet." The map has as many doors as there are people, and every door opens onto the whole. This matters most for minds that were told they'd learned things in the wrong order, or hadn't earned the next rung. In a rhizome there are no rungs — only the next connection that makes sense to you. No prerequisite. No gatekeeper. As many doors as there are people. A Mycelium and a Rhizome · Stimpunks

The network flows The mycelium moves A rhizome is the shape; a mycelium is the life in it. Underground, fungal threads lace through the soil and trade with the roots they meet — water and scarce minerals for sugar made in the light. Whether those threads also wire whole forests together, elder tree feeding shaded seedling — the "wood wide web" (Simard) — is the contested part, and we hold it loosely (Karst, Jones & Hoeksema, 2023). And the network is not fixed. Where a path is useful, traffic thickens it; where it isn't, it quietly fades. A slime mold — one cell, no brain, no boss — grows across a map of scattered food and settles into almost exactly the rail network human engineers drew for Tokyo (Tero et al., 2010). Decentralised, and still smart. That's how care and knowledge move through our communities too: not issued from a head office, but flowing along the threads to wherever they're needed, strengthening whatever works. Not issued from a head office — flowing along the threads to wherever it's needed. the network learns plenty fed in the shade strong paths thicken · weak paths fade flow · redistribute · adapt smart without a boss A Mycelium and a Rhizome · Stimpunks

same shape, different scale cosmic web mycelium neuron not a pyramid — a web supercluster · mushroom · synapse read the captions to tell them apart the universe's favourite shape Every scale The same shape everywhere Zoom all the way out and the shape returns. The cosmic web — the largest structure there is — is galaxies strung like dew along vast filaments of dark matter, with great voids between and no center anywhere. Matter drifts down the strands to the bright knots where filaments cross. Set a slice of the cosmic web beside a mycelial mat, beside a slime mold, beside a single neuron, and you have to read the captions to tell them apart. The universe keeps reaching for the same answer: not a pyramid, a web. So when we build without a throne at the top, we aren't failing to organise. We're organising the way the universe does at every scale. Decentralisation isn't disorder — it's the oldest structure there is. Not a pyramid. A web. The oldest structure there is. The Autistic Rhizome is "a network with no single point of origin. No part of the network depends upon the existence of another." No advocates ranked above followers, no advancing by how much you know — we meet as equals, held together by a do-no-harm ethic instead of a chain of command. Helen Edgar maps the same ground: watering holes and Discords alive at 2am, belonging you don't have to earn. Lose any one node and the network lives on, because nothing depends on a center.
