It is genuinely remarkable — and it is not the summit of a hierarchy. The elephant has more neurons; the crow packs them denser; the octopus spreads them through its arms; the slime mold does without. This is where the guide lands. We kept holding every nervous system up against our own and naming the difference "deficit" — the same move, scaled across species, that pathologises a divergent human mind. There is no standard nervous system. Ours included. (See Not a Line and Every Nervous System.) Trait Sounds like Actually A large neocortex the pinnacle of minds one design among many that work ~86 billion neurons the most that matters the elephant has three times as many The measure of "intelligence" the standard a standard we wrote, then graded everyone by Its way not the standard — one way among many · L★S 011

3 Field Guide Stimpunks Foundation · Zine No. 3 A field guide to the Neurodiversity Paradigm What the paradigm actually claims. What it means to say variation instead of disorder. Why the universe doesn't pathologize its own variation — and why that matters. The paradigm, plainly stated Neurodiversity · InLv · Nick Walker open edition L★S
Two frameworks.One is a medical model.One is a paradigm.

Two ways of seeing · the same person Two frameworks. One is a medical model. One is a paradigm. The neurodiversity paradigm doesn't replace medicine. It changes the frame — what counts as a problem, who gets to define it, and what solutions are even on the table. Here are the two frameworks, side by side. Pathology Paradigm Neurodiversity Paradigm Neurological difference is a disorder — a deviation from normal functioning that needs to be identified and treated. Neurological difference is a form of natural variation — one point in the full range of human neurological experience. The goal is to identify what is wrong with the person and move them closer to a neurotypical standard. The goal is to understand the person's actual profile and create conditions where they can thrive as they are. Difficulty is located inside the person — as a deficit, a symptom, a dysfunction. Difficulty is located in the mismatch between the person and their environment — the environment is often the problem. Success means the person appears more neurotypical — masks better, behaves more normatively. Success means the person can live well as themselves — with support that fits their actual needs. The diagnostic manual defines the standard from which the person has deviated. The diagnostic manual is a tool for accessing support — useful but not definitive of who a person is. The person's way of being in the world is a problem to be solved. The person's way of being in the world is a valid mode of human existence. Neurodiversity Field Guide · Stimpunks
Not a buzzword.A paradigm witha lineage.

The word · its history Not a buzzword. A paradigm with a lineage. The concept of neurodiversity emerged from the Autistic community in the 1990s — not from academia, not from clinicians, but from Autistic and neurodivergent people describing their own experience and organizing around it. The online community InLv (Independent Living on the Autistic Spectrum), founded by Martijn Dekker in 1996, was one of the primary spaces where this thinking developed. Jim Sinclair's foundational essay "Don't Mourn For Us" (1993) and the work of Autism Network International laid the groundwork. The ideas were built through collective lived experience — no single author, and no one handing them down. This history matters. The paradigm was not handed down from above. It was built from the inside — by the people it describes, from their own understanding of themselves. That is its authority. The definition · plainly stated Neurodiversity (the paradigm) Neurodiversity is the infinite variation in neurocognitive functioning within our species — the diversity of human minds. The paradigm holds that this variation is natural and valuable, that there is no one "normal" brain any more than there is one normal ethnicity, and that neurological differences — autism, ADHD, dyslexia, and others — are not deficits to be cured. Some of that divergence is innate; some is made by experience. Neither kind is an error. — after Nick Walker, Neuroqueer Heresies (2021) Neurodivergent Having a mind that functions in ways which diverge significantly from the dominant societal standards of "normal." Not a synonym for disabled — though many neurodivergent people are disabled. A description of neurological difference, not a diagnosis. — term coined by Kassiane Asasumasu (2000); definition after Nick Walker, Neuroqueer Heresies (2021) Neurotypical Having a neurological profile that aligns with dominant societal standards of "normal." Not a synonym for healthy or good — a description of one position in the neurological distribution. Neurodiversity Field Guide · Stimpunks
The DSM isa tool.Not a truth.

Diagnosis · what it is and isn't The DSM is a tool. Not a truth. The neurodiversity paradigm is not anti-diagnosis. Diagnoses unlock support, accommodations, language, and community. For many people, getting a diagnosis is a profound relief — finally having a word for what their life has been. What the paradigm disputes is the idea that the DSM defines reality — that the categories it creates are natural kinds rather than constructed tools. Diagnostic criteria are written by committees, revised every decade or so, and shaped by cultural assumptions about what counts as "normal" functioning. The DSM describes what deviates from a norm. The paradigm asks: who sets the norm? Who benefits from it? What gets missed when the instrument is calibrated only to detect deviation? Common misreadings · corrected Myth "The neurodiversity paradigm says autism/ADHD isn't real." Fact The paradigm says neurological differences are real — and that framing them as disorders rather than variations changes what we see and what we do. Myth "It only applies to people who are 'mildly' affected." Fact The paradigm applies across the full range of neurological difference — including people with high support needs. Support needs and human value are separate questions. Myth "Neurodiversity means you can't acknowledge that things are hard." Fact The paradigm locates difficulty precisely — in the mismatch between a person and their environment, not in the person's existence. That's a more accurate and more useful place to intervene. Myth "It's just positive spin — trying to make people feel good about deficits." Fact It's a substantive claim about the nature of neurological variation, grounded in disability theory, lived experience, and increasingly, in neuroscience. The goal is accuracy, not reassurance. Myth "If we don't call it a disorder, people won't get help." Fact The paradigm fully supports appropriate support and accommodation — it changes the justification, not the outcome. You don't need to call someone broken to give them what they need. Neurodiversity Field Guide · Stimpunks

The core reframe The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation. This is not a metaphor borrowed from cosmology for comfort. It is a precise statement about the relationship between variation and value. The universe produces variation at every scale — in stellar types, in orbital mechanics, in the distribution of matter, in the neurological profiles of its most complex structures. No variation in that distribution is intrinsically wrong. The concept of "disorder" requires a norm, and norms are always constructed by someone, for some purpose, from some position. When the calcium in your bones was forged in a dying star, the universe did not ask whether it was being made correctly. It was matter becoming what matter becomes. Your neurology is the same. It is the universe producing variation — which is what the universe does. The paradigm takes this seriously. It says: difference is not deficit. Variation is not disorder. The distribution is not a hierarchy. Five principles · the paradigm in practice Principle 01 Neurological variation is natural Human neurological profiles exist on a distribution. No point on that distribution is intrinsically correct. Autism, ADHD, dyslexia, and related profiles are not errors — they are positions in a natural range. Principle 02 Disability is often environmental Much of what makes neurodivergence disabling is the mismatch between a person's profile and an environment designed for a narrower range. Change the environment and you change the disability. Principle 03 Support needs don't determine worth Having high support needs is not a measure of human value. Every person, regardless of support needs, deserves to have those needs met and to be treated with full dignity. Principle 04 Autistic and neurodivergent people are the experts The people who live a neurological experience have knowledge about it that outside observers don't. The paradigm centers neurodivergent voices — particularly on questions about neurodivergent lives. Principle 05 Nothing about us without us Decisions about neurodivergent people should involve neurodivergent people. This applies to research, policy, education, clinical practice, and every other domain that shapes neurodivergent lives. Neurodiversity Field Guide · Stimpunks

The paradigm applied · lived experience What this changes The paradigm isn't only theoretical. It has practical consequences for how neurodivergent people understand themselves and how the people around them should respond. When you adopt the neurodiversity paradigm, certain things shift. The question changes from "what is wrong with this person?" to "what does this person need, and what is the environment failing to provide?" That shift has consequences. It changes what interventions look like. It changes what success looks like. It changes whether the goal is making someone appear more normal or helping them live well as who they are. It also changes how neurodivergent people are allowed to understand themselves — not as broken versions of a normal person, but as one valid configuration of the remarkable variation the universe produces. Practical implications 🔬 In assessment: The goal shifts from identifying deficits to mapping a full profile — strengths, challenges, and what environments and supports allow the person to thrive. 🏫 In education: Accommodation isn't charity — it's the environment doing its job. Universal design benefits everyone. The Autistic student asking for written instructions improves outcomes for the whole class. 🩺 In healthcare: Clinicians learn to ask neurodivergent patients how they experience their symptoms rather than assuming a neurotypical baseline. Sensory needs, communication differences, and masking are taken seriously. 👥 In community: Stimming is welcome. Atypical communication is met with curiosity, not correction. People are not asked to perform neurotypicality as the price of belonging. 💛 In self-understanding: You are not a failed version of a normal person. You are a valid configuration of the variation the universe produces. Your neurology belongs here. L★S. Neurodiversity Field Guide · Stimpunks

L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff No. 1 Bone Song — on piezoelectric matter & star-forged calcium No. 2 Love You Down To Your Star Stuff — the phrase, the elements, the scale No. 3 Neurodiversity Field Guide — the paradigm, plainly stated ← you are here Next We Are All Star Stuff — voices from the community The Neurodiversity Field Guide is the third zine in the Stimpunks series. It is offered freely, to be printed and folded and handed to someone who needs a clear statement of what the neurodiversity paradigm actually claims. The paradigm history draws on the foundational work of Autism Network International, Jim Sinclair's "Don't Mourn For Us" (1993), the Autistic community of InLv — Martijn Dekker's list, founded 1996 — and Nick Walker's Neuroqueer Heresies (2021), whose definitions of neurodiversity, neurodivergent and neurotypical this guide follows. The words neurodivergent and neurodivergence were coined by Kassiane Asasumasu (2000). The paradigm was developed by neurodivergent people from their own lived experience, not handed down from clinical or academic authority. The "nothing about us without us" principle has its roots in the broader disability rights movement, and reached disability studies in English largely through James I. Charlton's Nothing About Us Without Us (1998). The star stuff framing — the universe doesn't pathologize its own variation — connects this paradigm to the cosmological grounding of the full series. Your neurology and the calcium in your bones were made by the same universe. Neither one is wrong. a few neighbours · no captain 22 Emergence Stimpunks Foundation · Zine No. 22 No One Is the Leader on murmurations, emergence, and the whole that exceeds its parts — a flock has no captain, and neither does a self L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·

The murmuration No one is the leader At dusk, hundreds of thousands of starlings pour across the sky in one rolling, folding shape — splitting, pooling, turning inside out, all as if breathed by a single lung. Watch for an hour and you will never find the bird in charge, because there isn't one. The physics is almost unbearably simple. Each starling attends to only its six or seven nearest neighbours — not a fixed distance but a fixed few companions (Ballerini and the STARFLAG project, 2008). Match their heading, hold your spacing, turn when they turn. That local rule, run by every bird at once, is the entire program. From it: a whole that no bird intends, no bird can see, and no bird commands. Order without a ruler. This has a name — emergence — and once you have seen it, you start seeing it everywhere. Look for the bird giving orders. There is none. That absence is the miracle. one bird tracks seven — the sky moves as one seven neighbours, no captain local rules, global shape No One Is the Leader · Stimpunks

the parts every rule, listed more something new knowing the parts does not rebuild the whole more is different the whole is not the sum reduction doesn't run backwards Anti-reductionism More is different In 1972 the physicist Philip Anderson gave this its clearest statement, in an essay called More Is Different. Take reality apart and you find simpler laws — atoms, then particles, all the way down. But the reverse fails: knowing every rule the parts obey does not let you predict, or rebuild, the whole they make. At each new level of scale, entirely new properties, patterns, and laws appear that simply aren't present in the parts. Wetness isn't in one water molecule. Life isn't in one atom. The murmuration isn't in one starling. You don't get them by adding; you get them by relating. Reductionism took the world apart to name it — and then handed us the pieces as if they were the thing. But the whole was never more of the parts. It was something different. The whole isn't more of the parts. It's different from them. — after P. W. Anderson, "More Is Different," 1972 No One Is the Leader · Stimpunks

Structure formation The universe self-organised The largest structures there are did exactly the same thing. The infant universe was almost perfectly smooth — but not quite. Faint ripples of denser and emptier, printed into the cosmic microwave background, were the whole seed. Gravity did the rest. Denser patches pulled a little harder, drew in a little more, pulled harder still. Over billions of years matter drained out of the voids and strung itself along threads, until the whole cosmos had woven the cosmic web — galaxies beaded along filaments around enormous bubbles of empty space. No architect drew it. No first galaxy gave the order. Gravity plus a whisper of unevenness, run everywhere at once, was enough. The cosmic web is a murmuration written in gravity — turning so slowly we mistake it for a plan. No blueprint. No architect. Just gravity, a little unevenness, and time. void galaxies on filaments · voids between the cosmic web a flock frozen in gravity No One Is the Leader · Stimpunks

the checklist deficits counted the whole the parts don't add up to you you exceed them a person is an emergence realer than the list The whole person You are not a checklist Here is the first thing the flock teaches. A diagnosis is a list of parts: traits itemised, deficits counted, boxes ticked against a baseline. Useful, sometimes. But you can no more rebuild a person from that list than rebuild a murmuration from one bird's rules. A person is what emerges — a whole that is different from, and realer than, the sum of the criteria. The checklist is the parts. You are the murmuration. This is difference first in a new key: not a defective version of a standard human, but a whole that no inventory of missing pieces could ever contain. When a system reduces you to a score, it has confused the feathers for the flight. More is different — and you are the more. A checklist of deficits is a pile of feathers. You are the flock in flight. No One Is the Leader · Stimpunks

org chart orders down a chain competency network eye-level · trust · gifts decisions where the knowledge already lives flock, not hierarchy nobody at the top NeurodiVentures A murmuration, not an org chart The second thing the flock teaches is how we gather. Our healthiest collectives — NeurodiVentures — run like murmurations, not org charts: no boss at the top passing orders down a chain, but competency networks and catalysts rather than leadership and leaders. The local rules are few — everyone teaches and learns, trust extended first, decisions made where the knowledge already lives. From them, a collective intelligence emerges that no single mind could hold. Hierarchy hoards the privilege of not needing to learn; a flock keeps everyone attending to their neighbours. Nota leader to find — no bird carries the plan. Notan org chart — a competency network, a map of gifts. Notorders from the top — decisions where the knowledge lives. Nota hero or a lone genius — a whole no single part contains. No One Is the Leader · Stimpunks

many birds · one figure no one drew it · all of them made it the whole, arriving star stuff, self-assembling The whole The whole is the miracle Bring it together. Starlings, the cosmic web, a mind, a movement — one pattern runs through all of them: put enough parts into relation and something arrives that no part contains and no ruler commands. That something new is not noise to be reduced away. It is the whole point. You are not a set of deficits managed by a captain in your head — you are an emergence, whole and in motion. And we, together, are not an org chart waiting on a leader — we are a murmuration, turning as one because we tend to the few beside us. No one is the leader. That was never a lack. It's how star stuff has made every ordered thing it has ever made — including you, including us. More is different. You are the more. We are the more. No One Is the Leader · Stimpunks

What are the few local rules — the neighbours you attend to — that let your people move as one? Where are you waiting for a leader, when what you need is a murmuration? No One Is the Leader is the twenty-second zine in the Stimpunks series, and it names the principle that quietly runs under the whole collection: order without a ruler. Its spine is emergence — Philip W. Anderson's "More Is Different" (Science, 1972), the founding statement of anti-reductionism: at each level of scale, new laws appear that the parts don't contain, so knowing the parts never rebuilds the whole. The science: starling murmurations and the finding that each bird tracks a fixed number of nearest neighbours — roughly six or seven — rather than a fixed distance (Ballerini et al., the STARFLAG project, PNAS 2008), the topological rule from which flocking self-organises (with an early nod to Craig Reynolds' 1986 "boids"); and cosmic structure formation — primordial density fluctuations imprinted in the cosmic microwave background, amplified by gravitational instability into the cosmic web of filaments and voids. Two murmurations, one made of birds and one made of galaxies, neither with an architect. The lived knowledge: non-hierarchical, self-organising neurodivergent collectives — NeurodiVentures (Jorn Bettin; Autistic Collaboration, autcollab.org), built with competency networks in place of leadership and hierarchy (Laloux 2014; Bettin & Elliffe 2016), where power is understood as "the privilege of not needing to learn" and omni-directional learning keeps everyone both teaching and learning. adrienne maree brown's Emergent Strategy (2017) reads the murmuration as organising wisdom, and we follow her lead. The whole-person reading rests on the neurodiversity paradigm (Nick Walker) and our own Why Difference Comes First (No. 11). Held with care: leaderless is not structureless — a murmuration is intensely organised, it simply has no ruler; self-organising is not chaos, and distributing decisions is not abandoning support or accountability. The star stuff is Carl Sagan's, and the SN 1006 remnant on every Stimpunks page. The reading — that no one is the leader, and that this was never a lack — is ours. You were an emergence, whole and in motion, all along. no clock the universe keeps 19 Time Stimpunks Foundation · Zine No. 19 No Universal Now on relativity, crip time, and the clock that was never the universe's — with a coda by Helen Edgar L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·

Relativity No master clock Newton assumed one universal time, ticking the same everywhere — a single clock the whole cosmos runs by. For two centuries it seemed obvious. It's also wrong. Einstein showed that simultaneity is relative: two events that happen "at the same time" for me can happen at different times for you, if we're moving differently. Worse for the master clock — time itself runs slower the faster you travel, and slower again the deeper you sit in gravity. This isn't a thought experiment: the GPS in your phone only works because engineers correct for the satellites' clocks ticking faster than clocks on the ground. There is no clock the universe checks against. Every clock keeps its own honest time. The universe keeps no master clock. Why should you? an event A · now B · now time ↑ two observers, two "nows" simultaneity is relative No Universal Now · Stimpunks

9 · 10 · 11 · 12 stamped onto bodies & minds railway time · factory time a convention, not a law Standard time The clock is a human invention So if nature keeps no universal now, where did the one true clock come from? We built it. Synchronized clock time — the shared minute, the timetable, the standardized zones — is barely a century and a half old, an agreement stitched together for railways and factories so trains would not collide and shifts would start together. It is genuinely useful. But it is a convention, not a law of physics — and somewhere along the way we forgot we invented it and began treating it as reality itself, then measuring bodies and minds against it. Be productive on its schedule; wake, work, and rest on its count. The clock stopped being a tool and became a judge. You can't fail a law of nature. You can only fail to fit a rule someone wrote. We built the clock, then mistook it for the sky. No Universal Now · Stimpunks

Crip time Crip time bends the clock Disabled people have a name for living off that clock: crip time. Irving Zola and Carol Gill were among the first to write it into disability studies — a term already alive in the community; it means the extra time and the flexible time — arriving at various intervals, processing at various rates, needing more hours or fewer or simply other ones. The usual reading is that we are failing to keep up. Crip time says the opposite: the schedule was built narrow, and a body meeting it late is information about the schedule. As Alison Kafer puts it, rather than bend disabled minds and bodies to the clock, crip time bends the clock to meet disabled minds and bodies. Which is exactly the move of Minor Worlds: don't fix the person — change the thing around them. Here the thing is time itself. Rather than bend the body to the clock, bend the clock to the body. — after Alison Kafer bend the body to the clock bend the clock to the body room to move same body, two clocks flex time, exploded No Universal Now · Stimpunks

clock time spiral time a smell pulls a thread across decades not a line — a spiral time folds back on itself Monotropic time Spiral time, felt time For many neurodivergent people, time was never a line to begin with. In a monotropic attention tunnel it stretches and folds — an hour of flow vanishes; a bad ten minutes lasts a week. Memory works the same way: not a shelf of dated files but a spiral you re-navigate, where a smell tugs a thread across decades and yesterday can feel further off than childhood. Marta Rose named this spiral time; Helen Edgar, writing of felt time, describes how a moment from years ago might feel like now, while a conversation from yesterday feels distant. It's why "what did you do last weekend?" can land as a demand rather than a question. Not broken clock-reading — a different clock, measured in intensity, not minutes. Bergson called this lived duration; physics, in its own tongue, already agreed that duration bends. Remembering isn't recall. It's re-navigation. — Helen Edgar, More Realms No Universal Now · Stimpunks

Six ways of looking Time travel, broken time None of this is only lovely. Ellen Samuels, in Six Ways of Looking at Crip Time, holds the hard edges too. Crip time is time travel — a wormhole of jerky stops and starts that pulls you out of the tidy line of life-stages, so you meet the frailties of old age while young, or get treated as a child at any age. It is grief time and sick time: the days that swell around a loss, the strange arithmetic where you must earn the very hours in which to be ill. Capacity arrives and departs on its own schedule, and the clock offers no credit for it. So we hold both at once — the flexibility is a gift, and the brokenness is real. Naming it plainly is how we stop grading ourselves against a straight line we were never on. Notlate — keeping a different, honest time. Notbehind — we were never on your line. Notlazy or slow — running a clock the wall can't read. Nota schedule to be fixed to — a schedule that should bend to us. the expected line crip time stops · starts · loops · gaps a wormhole, not a timeline held: gift and grief at once No Universal Now · Stimpunks

many clocks · no master each keeps its own time and none is late Arrive where we started Star stuff keeps its own time So here is the whole of it. The cosmos runs on countless clocks and no master; so do we. The wall clock is a fine tool and a terrible judge, and it never was the sky. T.S. Eliot wrote of arriving where we started and knowing the place for the first time — the shape of spiral time, and of star stuff, which is forged, scattered, and gathered back into new forms that remember. You are made of atoms billions of years old, keeping time no watch can hold. You were never late. There is no schedule to be late to — only your own true time, which the universe has kept, patiently, since the first star. Made of star stuff, you keep the oldest time there is — your own. No Universal Now · Stimpunks

Coda a guest passage by Helen Edgar · Autistic Realms / More Realms Memories scatter like shards of seaglass along a fractured spiral, the centre always slipping just beyond my grasp. Remembering isn't straightforward for me; it's less recall and more a process of re-navigation. Time folds back in on itself. A moment from years ago might feel like now, while a conversation from yesterday feels distant or unretrievable — unless something hooks me in and brings it back into focus. My memories don't line up neatly. They tangle, twist, merge, and drift like mist through a forest. Sometimes I'm not remembering in the traditional sense at all, but kind of re-sensing — a texture, a tone of voice, the way the light fell. It can be disorienting, in a world that expects time and memory to be neat and logical. But it is also a kind of richness, a depth of connection that linear systems miss. We shall not cease from exploration — and arrive where we started, and know the place for the first time. — Helen Edgar · on felt time & monotropic memory · morerealms.com closing line after T.S. Eliot, Four Quartets No Universal Now · Stimpunks

a fingerprint, not a ladder 21 Spectrum Stimpunks Foundation · Zine No. 21 Not a Line on spectra, constellations, and why "mild to severe" was always the wrong picture — after Helen Edgar & Patrick Dwyer L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·

Spectroscopy A spectrum is not a line Split white light through a prism and you don't get a ranking from a bad end to a good end. You get a fan of every wavelength at once — red through violet, none higher or lower, just light spread out by colour. Now split the light of a star. Threaded through its spectrum are fine dark and bright lines — and here's the wonder: every element leaves its own exact pattern of them, a fingerprint. Hydrogen signs one way, helium another, iron another still. Reading those lines is the only way we know what the stars are made of. So a spectrum was never a scale of more-or-less. It is a signature of what something is made of. A spectrum doesn't rank a star. It tells you what the star is made of. every wavelength hydrogen iron each element, its own fingerprint a fan, then a signature this is how we read the stars Not a Line · Stimpunks

mild severe where are you? the line of neuronormativity one axis · one ranking the picture we were handed a ladder, not a fingerprint The severity scale But we heard a line Then the word crossed into talk about autism, and something was lost in translation. Spectrum got heard as a line: mild at one end, severe at the other, everyone slotted somewhere between. High-functioning here, low-functioning there. "A little bit Autistic." "We're all somewhere on it." Patrick Dwyer names the problem plainly: a single line from "highest" to "lowest functioning" erases how the same person struggles more or less in different domains, on different days, in different rooms. And functioning labels don't just mislead — they gatekeep, sorting us into "not disabled enough" to deserve support or "too disabled" to be trusted with our own choices. The word meant fingerprint. We heard ladder. "Mild to severe" measures how much you inconvenience us — not who you are. Not a Line · Stimpunks

The spiky profile Better — but still a grid Many of us met a better picture: the spiky profile. Not uniformly mild or severe but jagged — high in some domains, low in others, peaks and troughs across social, sensory, cognitive, and motor. It kills the single dial, and that matters. But as Helen Edgar points out, the spiky profile still plots us on a grid. It reads our peaks and dips as distances from a flat, expected baseline — the line of neuronormativity — frozen at one moment of assessment. A better chart is still a chart of how far we fall from normal. It traded one line for a row of them. Progress — but still a grid, and still a baseline we're measured against. The spiky profile stopped ranking us on one line — and started ranking us on many. baseline peaks & troughs — measured from the line jagged, but still plotted a better chart is still a chart Not a Line · Stimpunks

no axis · no baseline · no rank a figure, not a score read from where you stand The constellation A constellation, not a chart So drop the grid entirely. Patrick Dwyer offers a different figure: an autism constellation — not a point on a scale but many stars in many positions, each Autistic person a different arrangement of them. Helen Edgar carries it further: a constellation of intensities. Not points plotted on a chart but an interdependent, monotropic galaxy — sensory, cognitive, and relational ways of being in ever-shifting relation. A constellation has no baseline and no rank; its stars sit at wildly different distances and cohere into a figure only from where you happen to stand. Relational, contextual, alive. That is us: not a measurement, but a pattern of light. always in motion, always connecting, always becoming — never fixed, never finished. — Helen Edgar Not a Line · Stimpunks

no baseline to measure from free of the ruler no norm star Difference first No line, no centre, no norm Here is what a constellation quietly refuses. With no line, there's no top to reach and no bottom to fall to — and no centre either. The whole machinery of functioning levels assumed a norm to measure our distance from. A constellation has no norm star. This is the frame we keep returning to: difference comes first. Difference isn't deviation from a standard human; the standard was a story we told — and then used to decide who got believed, supported, or dismissed. And — this matters — refusing the line is not refusing that some of us need far more support. It refuses that support needs rank us. The honest replacement for a label was never a better label; it's naming the specific support each of us actually needs. No line. And still, all the care. Nothigh- or low-functioning — labels that gatekeep support, not descriptions of us. Notmild or severe — a fingerprint has no volume knob. Not"a little bit on the spectrum" — the spectrum was never a little-to-a-lot. Nota dial to be set — a constellation to be read. Not a Line · Stimpunks

each a fingerprint · together a constellation the two skies, at once signature and figure The whole light Every star its own spectrum Bring the two skies together. Read any star's light and you get not a rank but a fingerprint — this one rich in iron, that one in helium, each unmistakably itself. And no star sits on a line; they hang at every distance, making figures only a living eye can join. We are both at once: each of us a whole spectrum, a signature no one else carries — and together a constellation, a pattern that shifts with where we stand and who we stand among. The rainbow on every page of this site was never a ladder from red to violet. It's the whole light, arriving at once. This is what the creed meant all along: every colour, key, and frequency of neurodiversity. You are not high or low on anything. You are star stuff, reading itself. You are not a point on a line. You are a whole spectrum — a constellation no one has ever seen before. Not a Line · Stimpunks

L★S The spectrum was never a line from mild to severe. A spectrum is a fingerprint; the sky's figure is a constellation. You are not ranked — you are read. No. 15 Every Creature's Own Sky — umwelt, attention-worlds & double empathy No. 16 Minor Worlds — niche construction & the building of livable worlds No. 17 The Nearest Body — tides, co-regulation & being pulled by what's near No. 18 The Garden and the Stars — knowledge gardens, the commons & how star stuff knows itself No. 19 No Universal Now — relativity, crip time & the clock that was never the universe's No. 20 The Same Water — phase transitions, fluctuating capacity & changing the conditions No. 21 Not a Line — spectra, constellations & the end of the severity scale ← you are here Reflection Where have you been handed a functioning label — and what did it gatekeep? If you drew yourself as a constellation instead of a score, what would be in it? What specific support do you actually need — named, not ranked? Not a Line is the twenty-first zine in the Stimpunks series, and it argues for the metaphor Star Stuff already runs on: the sky is organised by constellations, not lines. It is built, with gratitude, on two pieces — Patrick Dwyer's "The Autism Constellation" (Autistic Scholar, 2020) and Helen Edgar's "The Constellation of Intensities: Neuroqueering the Spiky Profile" (Autistic Realms, 2026), whose line → spiky profile → constellation is this zine's spine. The metaphor is older than any one essay, and belongs to the Autistic community. Dwyer notes in a 2021 update that he did not coin it: Caroline Hearst had built a physical autism-constellation model and shown it at events, and the idea was already moving by word of mouth before that — with Larry Arnold an early proponent and Damian Milton and the late Dinah Murray discussing similar concepts. In correspondence with Helen Edgar, Milton credits Larry Arnold as the first he knows of to use "constellation" in place of "spectrum." We name them here because a zine against ranking people should not erase the people whose idea this is. The science: dispersion and the prism (Newton); the electromagnetic spectrum; spectroscopy and spectral lines (Fraunhofer; Kirchhoff & Bunsen), by which each element's fingerprint reveals what stars are made of; and the constellation as a relational, perspective-made figure. The lived knowledge: the critique of functioning labels as gatekeeping (Ollibean; the Autistic Self Advocacy Network; "Words That Wound," NeuroHub Community); the spiky profile; monotropism; and the difference-first frame of Helen Edgar's Why Difference Comes First (No. 11). Held with care: refusing the severity line does not deny that some of us need far more support — functioning labels harm precisely because they gatekeep it. The just alternative is naming specific support needs: no rank, and all the care. The star stuff is Carl Sagan's, and the SN 1006 remnant on every Stimpunks page. The reading — that you are a fingerprint and a constellation, never a point on a line — is ours. You were ★stuff, and a whole spectrum, all along. The physics Only in relation A particle, on its own, doesn't quietly hoard its properties in private. In Carlo Rovelli's relational quantum mechanics, a system's properties become definite only relative to another system it interacts with (Rovelli, 1996). There's no view from nowhere in which an electron already "has" its values, waiting to be read. What is real is what happens between systems. An honest caution before we go further: RQM is one interpretation of quantum theory among several, and physicists still argue it. We're not smuggling physics in to prove anything about people. We are noticing a rhyme, not collecting a proof. "There is no absolute, observer-independent description of a person that tells the whole truth about themselves." — Helen Edgar, We Are Made of Relations (2026) the same particle, two situations in isolation ? no fact of the matter in relation ↑ definite — for that system a value is something two systems have between them not something one holds alone Only in Relation · after Helen Edgar

count the outcomes two coins — distinct H H H T T H T T 4 two bosons — identical H H H T T T (H T = T H) 3 the missing 4th is the tell nature can't tell the two apart so it doesn't count them apart What is actually real Count the bosons Flip two coins and you get four outcomes — HH, HT, TH, TT — because the coins are distinct objects, so "heads-then-tails" and "tails-then-heads" are two different things. Do the same with two identical quantum particles — two bosons — and nature counts only three. The two mixed cases collapse into one, because there is no fact about which particle is which (Webster, 2026). That vanished fourth outcome is measurable, and it is the tell: what's fundamental isn't the standalone particle. It's the symmetry — the relation — that says these two can't be told apart. "What is fundamentally real are not particles as such, but rather the laws and symmetries … that govern their behaviour." — George Webster, IAI (2026) Only in Relation · after Helen Edgar

Relation before relata Made of each other Entangled particles can't be described one at a time. The pair carries correlations the parts simply don't have on their own — measure one and you've said something about the other, however far apart they've drifted. The physicist-philosopher Karen Barad calls this intra-action: not the meeting of two things that already exist separately, but a relation out of which the parts come to be distinct at all (Barad, 2007). The relation is first. The "things" are what it leaves behind. There's a word for the human version, one Helen draws from Barad: intradependence — not two finished people who later depend on each other, but selves made of each other from the start. Deeper than interdependence. We don't arrive as sealed units who only later reach out. We are, from the start, relations wearing the shape of a person. inter- vs intra- inter-action two wholes, then a link intra-action one relation, then parts the bond is the origin, not the bridge the parts are what the relation leaves behind made of each other Only in Relation · after Helen Edgar

what comes first difference · relation objects (late arrivals) first the differentiating, then the things the object is what got built The order of things Difference, then relation Reading the physics through Deleuze, George Webster puts the metaphysics plainly: "Objects do not come first and then differ; rather, objects emerge out of more fundamental processes of differentiation." — George Webster, reading Deleuze (2026) First there is difference and relation; the tidy, standalone object is the late arrival — the thing that gets built. It's the same move Star Stuff has made from the start in Why Difference Comes First: the measured, average "normal person" was never the ground floor. Difference is. Turn it one notch further and relation is. Only in Relation · after Helen Edgar

What it means for us The gap is two-way When an Autistic person and a non-Autistic person misunderstand each other, the old story put the deficit in one of them — the Autistic one. Damian Milton named the truer picture: the double empathy problem. The misunderstanding runs both ways — a mismatch between two differently-built minds, not a fault inside one (Milton, 2012). Relational physics says: of course it does. The trouble was never sitting inside a single object. It lives in the relation. Helen widens double empathy into DEEP — Dynamic, Embodied, Ecological, Political — because the mismatch isn't a static glitch between two heads. It's alive, bodily, environmental, and shaped by power. Change the lighting, the pace, the assumptions, the room — and the "deficit" you were measuring moves. It was in the relation all along. where the gap lives one mind another mind not one side — the space between double empathy, made DEEP a mismatch is a property of the pair it has no single owner Only in Relation · after Helen Edgar

the ARLES ladder Systems Environment Lived exp. Relational + Regulation Attention near the base — on purpose regulation lives inside the relational rung not a private skill Up the ladder Regulation is relational This is why, in Stimpunks' ARLES ladder, Relational sits near the base — and why Regulation lives inside it. Regulation isn't a skill you own privately and keep failing to deploy. We co-regulate: nervous systems settle, or don't, in relation to other bodies, other pacing, a room that holds us or doesn't. So the support that actually works doesn't try to repair an isolated person. It changes the relational field — the sensory environment, the pacing, the temporal texture, a community's capacity to hold different ways of being. If it's not working, it's not the person. It's the environment, the relationships, or the system. — Stimpunks · ARLES "We are not broken objects. We are relations, all of us still becoming." — Helen Edgar (2026) Only in Relation · after Helen Edgar

Held with care What we are not saying Relational physics rhymes with how we already know support works. It is not a licence for the traps that show up whenever "quantum" meets "people." Notquantum mysticism. No "quantum consciousness," no mind magically collapsing reality. In physics the "observer" is any system at all — a speck of dust will do. Not"everything is connected" as a vibe. This is a specific claim about how properties come to be, not a warm fog. Notdissolution into sameness. Being a relation doesn't melt you. Where two rivers meet they run braided for miles — one current, still distinct. The spiky profile survives the merge. Notphysics proving a politics. A rhyme, not a proof. Our belonging stands on its own; the physics only rhymes with it. Nota duty to stay connected. Relational doesn't mean always available. Some of us need less contact, not more — and need is not a rank. the confluence, not the blur one channel · two waters · still distinct relation is not erasure difference survives belonging Only in Relation · after Helen Edgar

we all share air 24 Air Stimpunks Foundation · Zine No. 24 Shared Air on breath, co-regulation, and the air we hold in common L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·

The atmosphere One ocean of air There is only one air. The atmosphere is a single, restless, well-mixed body — no walls inside it, no separate airs for separate people. What you breathe out drifts and spreads, and within a year or two it has circled the whole planet. A breath here becomes a breath everywhere. It mixes so completely that the numbers turn tender. One breath holds something like ten thousand billion billion molecules — so many that, once an old breath has scattered through the sky, your next lungful very likely carries a few atoms once breathed by people long gone, and by strangers on the far side of the Earth right now. We are not sipping from separate cups. We are all drinking from the same sky. We are all drinking from the same sky. one thin shell of air a breath here becomes a breath everywhere one connected body of air no separate skies Shared Air · Stimpunks

you tree O₂ → ← CO₂ each breathes what the other breathes out respiration ↔ photosynthesis breathing on opposite beats The reciprocal breath What the trees exhale Your breath is a conversation with the green world. You breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon; leaves do the mirror image — taking in your carbon, handing back oxygen. Inhale, exhale, inhale: the forest is breathing with you, on the opposite beat. And the oxygen itself is a gift older than animals. For most of Earth's history there was almost none to breathe — until cyanobacteria invented photosynthesis and, across the Great Oxidation Event some 2.4 billion years ago, slowly exhaled an entire breathable sky. Every lungful you take is the exhaust of ancient microbes, kept fresh by every plant since. Follow the atoms back further and they leave the planet: the oxygen and nitrogen in the air were forged in the hearts of stars. You breathe star stuff that life remade for life. Every breath is the exhaust of ancient life — forged first in stars. Shared Air · Stimpunks

Shared-air space The room we breathe together When we share a room, we don't just stand near each other — we breathe the same air, in and out, trading it between our bodies breath by breath. This is shared-air space: the literal, physical air we hold in common every time we're together in a room. And our bodies know it. Nervous systems in the same space read one another without being told — the pace of a breath, the set of a shoulder, the tone of a voice — and start to settle into a shared rhythm. A calm body near you slows your breathing; a braced one quickens it. We co-regulate through the air, mostly below noticing. A steady nervous system nearby can pull yours into rhythm. So shared-air space is never only chemistry. It is nervous-system space too. Whether the air feels safe — how loud, how bright, how crowded, whether you can breathe easy — decides whether the bodies in it can settle, or must stay on guard. Good air makes room to regulate; hostile air leaves everyone bracing alone. To share a room is to trade breath — and to tune our nervous systems to each other. two bodies · one air breathing into the same rhythm breath traded · rhythms settling co-regulation through the air Shared Air · Stimpunks

who senses the bad air first? clean dangerous → canary most people the alarm is information sensitive first · a signal, not a flaw read it, don't blame it Sensory sensitivity Listen to the canaries Miners once carried canaries underground. The little birds felt the bad air — the odourless gas, the thinning oxygen — long before any person could. Not because they were weak, but because they were sensitive: their alarm was information, and it saved lives. Many of us are the canaries of the shared room. We catch the perfume three desks away, the stale unmoved air, the cleaning-chemical sting, the fluorescent hum pressing on the skull. Our discomfort isn't fussiness or fragility — it's an early-warning system telling everyone the air has gone bad. The old mistake is to blame the bird: you're too sensitive. The wiser move is to read the signal and change the air. What's unbearable for the most sensitive is quietly wearing on everyone — so build it breathable for the canaries, and it's breathable for all. Don't blame the canary. Change the air. Shared Air · Stimpunks

The habitability question Habitable — and for whom? Shared air is only shared if everyone in it can breathe. So the phrase carries a harder question: habitable, and for whom? The same room is not the same for everyone. Fragrance, smoke, dust, idling exhaust, an airborne virus — the load lands unevenly, heaviest on disabled, chronically ill, and racialised people, and on those with the least power to leave. One person's ordinary afternoon is another's asthma attack, migraine, or infection. Too often the fix gets dumped on whoever is harmed: mask alone, sit by the door, send the email that starts "so sorry to be difficult." That's backwards. Breathable air is a commons — a collective responsibility, not a private accommodation one person has to quietly manage. Shared air is only shared if everyone in it can breathe. the same room scent · smoke · virus fine can't breathe the burden falls unevenly same room · different air habitable, for whom? Shared Air · Stimpunks

open window plant mask CR box clean air, built and shared infrastructure as resistance window · plant · mask · filter box mutual aid you can build Solarpunk Move quietly and plant things Here's the hopeful part, and it's buildable. Clean, welcoming air isn't a luxury or a wish — it's infrastructure. Open a window. Add a plant. Wear the mask. Run a Corsi–Rosenthal box — a box fan and a few furnace filters taped into a cube, scrubbing a room's air for the price of a nice dinner. Mutual aid you can build in an afternoon. This is solarpunk: not "move fast and break things" but move quietly and plant things — a future with a human face and dirt behind its ears, where infrastructure is a form of care and hope is something you assemble, together, out of ordinary parts. We don't make air habitable by asking people to need less. We make it habitable by building better rooms — and sharing the how. Not"too sensitive" — the canary isn't fragile; its alarm is information. Nota private accommodation — habitable air is a commons, and a shared responsibility. Notextraction — we move quietly and plant things; we don't move fast and break lungs. Notscarcity — breathable, welcoming space isn't rationed; it's built and shared. Shared Air · Stimpunks

forged in stars leaf breath sky star · leaf · lung · sky held, then passed on The oldest breath The oldest breath Take one slow breath. The nitrogen in it is nearly as old as the Earth; the oxygen was exhaled by microbes before there were eyes to see them, and by a tree somewhere this morning. The atoms were cooked in stars that died before the Sun was lit. This air has been storm and birdsong and other people's words — and it will be again. You don't own it. You couldn't. You hold each breath for a moment and pass it on — to the person beside you, the tree down the street, a stranger not yet born. Breathing is the quietest proof that we were never separate. So share the air, and make it good. We all breathe the same star stuff, in and out, in common. Love you down to your star stuff. You hold each breath for a moment and pass it on. We were never separate. Shared Air · Stimpunks

L★S There is only one air — old, borrowed, forged in stars and remade by life. Every room we share is a shared-air space, where we trade breath and settle one another's nervous systems. Keeping that air breathable is something we owe each other, not a favour anyone should have to beg for. Where is your most breathable space — a shared-air room, a screen, somewhere else? What makes it so? In a room you share, who bears the cost of the air — and how could that be carried together? Shared Air is the twenty-fourth zine in the Stimpunks series, and a companion to Bodies of Water (No. 23): water and air, the two commons we can't opt out of. Shared-air space is a term coined by Helen Edgar and Ryan Boren; here it stands on its most physical ground — the literal air we share in a room, where nervous systems co-regulate breath by breath (see also The Nearest Body, No. 17). The neurodivergent reframe is ours and our kin's too: sensory sensitivity as an early-warning signal rather than a flaw — the "miner's canary," long taken up by disabled, chronically ill, and environmental-illness communities who name themselves the canaries of a world whose air has gone bad. Together they ask: habitable, and for whom? The ethos is solarpunk: adrienne maree brown, Emergent Strategy (2017), on interdependence and collective care; Adam Flynn's "Solarpunk: Notes toward a manifesto" (2014), for "a future with a human face and dirt behind its ears"; and the movement slogan "move quietly and plant things" (Andrew Dana Hudson). radio light carried across the dark 25 Signal Stimpunks Foundation · Zine No. 25 Shared Signal on distance, the clearer channel, and the rhythm we carry when we can't share a room L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·

The spectrum One field of signal Tune a radio, warm your hands at a fire, catch a sunburn, sit for an X-ray — every time, you are using the same single thing. Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays are not different substances. They are one electromagnetic field, vibrating at different speeds. Radio is only light too slow and long for our eyes; colour is just the signal our eyes happen to catch. So there is no ladder of realness running from "in person" at the top down to "mere signal." There is one continuous spectrum, and we live our whole lives inside it. The voice on a call and the light off a face across a table are the same phenomenon, cut at different wavelengths. One field. No separate signals — no more than there are separate airs. Radio and starlight are the same thing, cut at different wavelengths. one continuous field long / slow short / fast radio· your call infrared· fire visible· a face X / γ· a scan same wave · different wavelength radio · fire · colour · a scan one spectrum, end to end Shared Signal · Stimpunks

encode → send → decode encode decode a voice, folded onto a wave the mirror of exhale & inhale transmit · receive breath, timestamped and sent Transmit · receive The reciprocal signal Every signal is a two-sided act, the way every breath is. One body encodes — folds a voice, a word, a feeling onto a wave — and another decodes it back into meaning. Transmit and receive: the mirror of exhale and inhale. And what rides the wave is more than information. Voice carries breath — the pace of a sentence, the pause before a hard word, the exhale under a laugh, sent unedited. A voice note is breath, timestamped and sent. You aren't only receiving data; you're receiving someone's nervous system, encoded in sound. The physics doesn't care how far. The same law that carries your voice to a friend across the country carries a star's light across the galaxy. Encode, send, decode — it is how the universe has always passed itself along. A voice note is breath — timestamped, and sent. Shared Signal · Stimpunks

A term Helen coined Shared-signal space Shared-air space is the room — proximity, breath, nervous systems settling into one another's rhythm. It needed a counterpart. Not a lesser one. Helen Edgar named it: shared-signal space — connection carried on a signal instead of on the air of a room. A call, a message, a voice note, a synthesised voice: the rhythm still crosses, only now over distance. Does it really carry? Measurably, yes. The tone and pace of a voice cue safety below awareness (Porges, 2011), and that cueing doesn't stop at the edge of a screen: two people's heart-rhythms fall into sync even when they meet remotely — in shared virtual space, at levels comparable to being in the same room (Streuber et al., 2026). Some channels are thinner than that — a laggy call, a dropped word, text with no voice at all — and still the rhythm crosses. Distance can thin the channel. It does not empty it. And for many of us the signal-carried channel is where regulation and honest connection come easiest. Distance thins the channel. It does not empty it. co-regulation, carried in the room over signal thinner amplitude · same rhythm the rhythm still crosses thinner, but real Shared Signal · Stimpunks

live speech reply now tone, live no record all at once text · AAC … thinking time a saved record reread · revise thinking time · a record · fewer demands the thought, let through Text & AAC The clearer channel For many Autistic people, the written word isn't a downgrade from speech — it's the channel that finally lets the thought through. Text takes away the real-time crush: no instant reply owed, no tone to decode on the fly, no face to read while hunting for words. A message can be drafted, reread, and fixed before it's sent, so what lands is closer to what was meant. The largest survey of Autistic adults' own preferences found phone calls ranked last, again and again, and written channels near the top — for four steady reasons: thinking time, structure, fewer sensory demands, and a record to return to (Howard & Sedgewick, 2021). The same is true, and truer, of AAC. Symbol boards, letterboards, text-to-speech run through the written channel, not the spoken one. For non-speaking and minimally speaking people, AAC isn't a workaround bolted onto "real" communication. It is the real communication. Not a fallback from speech. For many of us, the version that finally lets the thought through. Shared Signal · Stimpunks

Anything but the phone Listen to the phone-averse "Anything but the phone!" is such a common Autistic refrain that researchers made it their title (Howard & Sedgewick, 2021). The live call asks for everything at once — instant response, tone read in real time, no record, no pause — and gives the least room to think. Dread of that channel isn't rudeness or fragility, any more than the canary's alarm was weakness. It's information: a signal that this channel is costly, and that a better one exists. Offer the text option and watch who suddenly comes through clearly. The fix isn't to toughen people up for phone calls. It's to stop treating one demanding channel as the toll for being reachable at all. Ask how someone would rather be reached — then reach them there. Aversion to a demanding channel is information, not fragility. how much a channel asks at once phone call instant · tone · no pause text paced · quiet · saved offer the other channel the aversion is a signal reach people where they come through Shared Signal · Stimpunks

no ladder — a rhizome watering holes · come & go sideways & underground lurking counts Reachable, and for whom? Build your own watering hole First the justice question, the twin of Shared Air's: reachable, and for whom? A signal life runs on data plans, devices, batteries, and platforms built by other people. When those cost too much or lock us out, "just message me" quietly excludes. Communication access is a commons, not a favour. So we build. The Autistic Rhizome (Edgar, 2026) spreads sideways and underground — no ladder, no single correct path: a Discord alive at 2am, a thread reopened after three years as if no time had passed, a reply to a stranger that becomes a friendship. Online spaces work as watering holes — loosely held, come-and-go, where presence alone can sustain connection. Lurking counts. One reply after months counts. Nobody handed us these rooms. We made them, and we keep them — infrastructure as mutual aid, in whatever medium lets us breathe. Nota fallback for when the room isn't available — a mode of connection, not a workaround. Notless true for being thinner — a thinner signal still carries a real rhythm. Notranked beneath presence — signal is a form of presence. exchange fungus plant L★S · 001 The Underground Exchange Fungi + plant roots · mutualism ~90% of land plants partner with fungi Fungal threads sheath and enter plant roots, trading the minerals and water they are good at gathering for the sugars the plant makes in the light. Underground, those threads reach far past anything a root could manage alone. mutualismthe wood wide webredistributionno one alone ▸ Field notes Field notes · Fungi + plant roots · mutualism Around nine in ten land plants live in partnership with mycorrhizal fungi. The fungus threads far further through the soil than any root could, gathering water and scarce minerals; the plant pays in sugar it makes from sunlight. Neither is doing charity — each is handing over what it has plenty of for what it lacks. Fungal threads do connect many plants at once, and the popular name for that is the "wood wide web" (Simard) — a sunlit elder feeding a seedling shaded on the forest floor. Be careful with this one: the root-to-fungus trade above is settled, but the forest-wide version is not. Reviewing the field studies, Karst, Jones & Hoeksema (Nature Ecology & Evolution 7, 2023) found the evidence too thin to say shared networks are widespread or that they reliably help seedlings, and found no published evidence that elder trees preferentially feed their own offspring through them. The lesson we keep is the smaller, sturdier one: not charity from the strong, but partners each handing over what they have plenty of. Monotropa uniflora, the ghost pipe, is the honest exception. It makes no chlorophyll and does no photosynthesis; it glows waxy-white in deep shade, living entirely on carbon it siphons from mycorrhizal fungi that are themselves fed by trees. Botanists call it a myco-heterotroph, or epiparasite: a one-directional relationship, not a mutualism. Named plainly, it belongs here precisely because not every symbiosis is gentle, or even. But read it with care. That a living thing takes what it needs and returns nothing in kind is not a moral failing — it is how a forest floor works, and how mutual aid works too: to each according to need. Some seasons, some bodies, can only receive, and the network holds them anyway. No one earns belonging through output; no one is disposable for being, this season, a taker. There's a deeper rhyme, too. "Monotropa" means one turn — the same root as monotropism, the Autistic attention-style (Murray, Lesser & Lawson, 2005). human the cosmos convenes 14 Council Stimpunks Foundation · Zine No. 14 The Council of All Beings on multispecies justice, more-than-human governance, and the star stuff that convenes L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·

Why a council The cosmos convenes Carl Sagan said it plainly: the calcium in our bones, the iron in our blood, forged in stars that died before the Earth was born. But the same is true of the soil under the city, the water in the river, the beaver and the cuckoo and the meadow. Every being at the table is star stuff. The Council of All Beings is a ritual from deep ecology, developed by Joanna Macy and John Seed: for an afternoon, humans set down the human mask and speak on behalf of another being — a mountain, a wolf, a river. Read cosmically, it isn't make-believe. It's the universe convening with itself, in all the forms it has learned to take. And that reframes everything downstream. You cannot rank what you are made of. Kinship here is not a metaphor — it's an inventory of shared atoms. The council is the universe convening with itself — the same star stuff, gathered in all the forms it has learned to take. one forge C · O · H Ca · Fe human beaver cuckoo river meadow same forge, different form every seat is star stuff The Council of All Beings · Stimpunks

justice count recognition be heard participation exist & act capabilities fair share distribution four questions for every being the agenda of a real council The seating chart Mere service providers The trouble is the seating chart we inherited. Modern planning treats the more-than-human world as a set of service providers — nature valued for what it yields to us, a resource rather than a relation. Repeated everywhere, that one move is a root of the socioecological crisis (Harms et al., 2025). Multispecies justice turns the resource back into a party with standing. It asks four plain questions of any being: can it count (recognition), can it be heard (participation), can it exist and act (capabilities), does it get a fair share (distribution)? These aren't abstractions. They're the agenda for a council that actually means to seat everyone. The Council of All Beings · Stimpunks

Ethodiversity Difference in how, not just what Biodiversity counts the kinds of life. But a subtler variety is nested inside it: not just what lives, but how it lives. Ombre Tarragnat calls this ethodiversity — the variety of "ways of being and behaving" across all animals — extending a term coined in ecology by Adolfo Cordero-Rivera. The migratory route, the dialect of a birdsong, the nocturnal life, the whole existential style of a creature. Its shadow is ethonormativity: the unwritten rule about which behaviours are allowed to count as acceptable. The horse who refuses the rider, the cat who won't be petted — abandoned, or worse, for departing from the expected script. A grid laid over a field that was already full of variation. So justice has to protect more than a list of species. It has to protect their ways of being. Star stuff varies in matter — and in manner. The council seats not just the beaver, but the beaver's way of being a beaver. The cosmos varies not only in what it makes, but in how its creatures live. Ethonormativity is the grid; ethodiversity is the field. the grid polices the ways of being ethonormativity over ethodiversity the field came before the grid The Council of All Beings · Stimpunks

the table SOIL BEAVER CUCKOO RIVER MEADOW a role card for every voice you argue the world from there Participation · the method Speak as the soil, the river How do you give a being a seat when it can't pull up a chair? You speak as it. In multispecies role-play — the method behind the guide Speaking as a River — people take the part of the soil, the beaver, the cuckoo, the meadow, and argue the world from there. One role card simply reads: "You are the Soil — without you, nothing works here." Good councils run on a few principles (after Artmann): each being is a relating subject with agency, not an object; each has a right to its own voice; each has value in itself, not only in use; and the exchange is reciprocal — giving and taking on equal terms, the old hierarchy set down. It's a rehearsal for a wider "we" — a room where the beaver's right to stay is something you answer to, not around. The Council of All Beings · Stimpunks

The hard part Who speaks, and how A borrowed voice carries a real hazard: speaking for a being can slide into speaking over it. A human voicing the river is, honestly, a human guess — shaped by human wants. Philosophical ethology offers a discipline for it. Vinciane Despret asks that we pose the questions that matter to the animal, not only to us; Jakob von Uexküll called each creature's lived world its Umwelt — the meadow a tick senses is not the meadow you see. The task is to enter that world, as far as you can, before you presume to represent it. Listen long. Represent second. Notventriloquism — a borrowed voice is a responsibility, not a costume. Maybe that's the truer shape of the thing. Not a table with seats around it, but a flow with all of us already in it — no head of the table, no order of speaking, just the same water finding its way through every body it passes. Not as a metaphor: the atoms in our bones were forged in stars that died before the Earth existed. Their ending is the reason we are here to look up at all. Ancestors work the same way. What they made — the free spaces, the strategies, the words — scattered outward when they were gone, and gathered into us. We don't start the fire. We catch its light. The bell curveis a vantage point

The same trick, on us The bell curve is a vantage point The curve that sorts us into normal and abnormal began in astronomy. It was the "error curve" — the math for how repeated measurements of a star's position scatter around its true one. In the 1800s, Adolphe Quetelet — an astronomer — turned that instrument on people, and invented l'homme moyen, the average man. What had described the error in a measurement now described the ideal human, with everyone else scattered around it as deviation. Francis Galton took the next step, reading the curve as a ranking, and built eugenics on it. So the tool that mapped the indifferent stars got turned on our minds — and the average, a made-up midpoint, was handed to us as the shape we were supposed to be. The Lines We Drew is the ninth zine in the Stimpunks series, and the companion argument to Field Guide No. 1 — where that guide redraws the constellations, this one is about why redrawing is legitimate at all. The astronomy is established. Orion's Belt is an asterism, not a physical group: Alnitak lies roughly 740 light-years away and Mintaka roughly 690, while Alnilam — the middle star — sits near 2,000 light-years, close to three times farther, so the belt's even spacing is an artifact of our line of sight (Museum of Science; APOD). Distances to these luminous, distant stars still carry real uncertainty, which only sharpens the point: even our instruments waver about a line we're sure we see. The lineage from stars to people is real and well documented. The bell curve entered science as the astronomer's "law of error": in his Theoria Motus (1809), Gauss used it to model how imperfect measurements scatter around a celestial body's true position — the same method that recovered the lost asteroid Ceres — with Legendre and Laplace close behind. Adolphe Quetelet, who directed the Brussels observatory, carried that error law from the sky to the census in his Essai de physique sociale (1835), inventing l'homme moyen, "the average man" — and, crucially, treating the average not as merely typical but as an ideal from which real people "deviate." Francis Galton kept Quetelet's curve but flipped its meaning: in Hereditary Genius (1869) he ranked human ability along what he called the "law of deviation from the average," graded groups above and below the line, and coined the word eugenics; his protégé Karl Pearson built the standard deviation and correlation as the first holder of the Galton Chair of Eugenics. The statistical sense of the word "normal" itself arrives in the mid-1800s alongside all of this. The sleight of hand was never the curve — some traits really are close to normally distributed — but the leap from deviation-as-measurement-error to deviation-as-human-defect, and the mistaking of a made-up midpoint for a law about how a person ought to be. Robert Chapman's Empire of Normality (2023) follows this same thread forward, into psychiatry and capitalism. On Chapman's account, Galton reframed the statistical centre as mere mediocrity rather than an ideal — so that deviation above it read as superiority and deviation below as defect — founding what Chapman calls the pathology paradigm: the frame, carried through Kraepelin into the DSM, that the neurodiversity movement later arose to name and refuse. The "normal" mind, in other words, has a history — and a contestable one. The border really does move: the American Psychiatric Association removed homosexuality from the DSM beginning in 1973; Asperger's disorder was added in DSM-IV (1994) and merged into Autism Spectrum Disorder in DSM-5 (2013). "Epistemic injustice," with its testimonial and hermeneutical forms, is Miranda Fricker's (2007). "Neurodiversity" was coined by Judy Singer (1998); the neurodiversity paradigm and its anti-pathology stance are articulated by Nick Walker and the wider community. The reading is ours: that the constructed line was never the sky, and so is ours to redraw. Further reading: Robert Chapman, Empire of Normality (Pluto, 2023); Stephen Stigler, The History of Statistics (1986); Theodore Porter, The Rise of Statistical Thinking (1986); Ian Hacking, The Taming of Chance (1990); Lennard Davis, Enforcing Normalcy (1995); Sarah Chaney, Am I Normal? (2022); and, for a general reader, Todd Rose, The End of Average (2016). Online: Fergus Murray, "Weird vs. Normal" (Weird Pride Day). Primary sources: Quetelet's Essai de physique sociale (1835) and Galton's Hereditary Genius (1869). Tidal force The near body wins The tide is the ocean answering to the sky. The Moon pulls hardest on the water directly beneath it, a little less on the rock of the Earth, less still on the far ocean — and that difference in pull, stretched across the planet, lifts a bulge on each side. Two bulges, turning under us: two high tides a day. Here is the strange part. The Sun is 27 million times more massive than the Moon, and it hauls on the Earth with over 170 times the raw force. Yet the Moon runs the tide. Tidal force falls off not with distance but with distance cubed — so the small, close body overwhelms the vast, far one. Distance matters more than mass. You are pulled most by what is nearest — not by what is largest. The Sun is 27 million times heavier. The Moon still owns the tide. Nearness beats mass. Phase transitions Water doesn't get gradually stiffer Cool a glass of water and it does not slowly thicken toward solid. It stays liquid, liquid, liquid — and then, at a single temperature, it flips all at once into ice. Not a gradual stiffening; a sudden change of state. It is the same H₂O on both sides — the very same molecules, only rearranged. Physicists call this a phase transition: a substance holding steady until a threshold in its conditions is crossed, then reorganising completely — solid, liquid, gas — with nothing added and nothing taken away. Nothing about the water got better or worse. It crossed a line. Nothing about the water changed. It crossed a line. state colder → liquid ice 0°C not a ramp — a cliff the flip happens all at once The Same Water · Stimpunks

pressure temperature → solid liquid gas one substance, many states the conditions decide The phase diagram The conditions, not the substance Whether that water shows up as ice, liquid, or steam depends entirely on the conditions around it — temperature and pressure. Scientists chart it on a phase diagram: a map with a region for each state and lines where one becomes another. Read it and the point lands quietly. Ice is not defective water; steam is not water trying harder. There is no best state and no failed state — only one substance, and the conditions it happens to be in. So if you want a different state, you change the conditions, not the substance. We said this once about rooms and minds. Here it is again, about states. Ice isn't broken water. It's water somewhere colder. The Same Water · Stimpunks

Fluctuating capacity Why could you do it yesterday? Here is the question so many of us brace for: why could you do it yesterday and not today? However kindly it's meant, it lands like a charge of inconsistency — as if yesterday proved today is a choice. The phase answer is simple. Capacity is a state, not a trait — and you were near a boundary. A little less sleep, one extra transition, a degree more noise, and the conditions tip. The same person crosses from managing to not managing, the way the same water crosses from liquid to ice on one degree of difference. Not unreliable. Not lazy. Not putting it on. The same you, in changed conditions. You are not inconsistent. You were near a boundary. coping overload + load one degree of difference same person, tipped by conditions a state, not a trait The Same Water · Stimpunks

Right at a phase boundary a substance turns turbulent and hypersensitive — tiny nudges cause wild swings, because it's poised between two states at once. That is threshold anxiety exactly: the dread that arrives before the crossing, the doorway harder than the room, the first day worse than the term. For a monotropic mind a transition means tearing attention out of one deep channel and re-forming it in another — and done suddenly, or piled up, it can pull the mind past what it can hold. So the fix isn't a sturdier person. It's a better crossing — built with warning, with a way back, with time. Broken thresholds, not broken people. Broken thresholds, not broken people. Weather-bodies Held past the point, slow to return Two more facts, because they name things that get misread. Water can be supercooled — held below freezing and still liquid — until one small disturbance crystallises the whole glass in an instant. That is the meltdown after a day that "went fine": not one trivial last straw, but a system kept past its limit, tipping all at once. And near a transition, systems show critical slowing down — they take far longer to settle after any knock. It isn't weakness that recovery swells near your edge; it's how systems behave there. Rest and regulation are the work, not a failure to do it. Ombre Tarragnat names us weather-bodies, always sensing and adjusting, and asks the better question: not how to make people more resilient to change, but how to make the climate more liveable. A smooth universeis a dead one

The cosmic scale A smooth universe is a dead one The early universe was almost perfectly uniform. Its oldest light — the cosmic microwave background — is smooth to about one part in a hundred thousand. Almost. Those faint differences, tiny ripples of denser and thinner, were the seeds. Gravity pulled the denser spots together, and over billions of years they grew into everything: stars, galaxies, planets, you. A perfectly uniform cosmos would have stayed a featureless fog forever — nothing to see, no one to see it. Structure exists because sameness broke. And the elements you are built from? monoculture blight one clone · one blight · total collapse polyculture many kinds · same blight · it holds variety is the resilient bet uniformity is efficient, and brittle The living scale Sameness is a single point of failure Nearly every banana shipped worldwide is a Cavendish — a sterile clone, grown from cuttings, all but genetically identical. One vast monoculture. It wasn't always. The export banana was the Gros Michel, until a fungus — Panama disease — wiped it out commercially by the 1960s. The industry survived only by switching to the Cavendish, which happened to resist that strain. Now a new strain, Tropical Race 4, is spreading, and the Cavendish has no defense. One clone, one blight from collapse. Biodiversity is the opposite bet: ecologists find more varied systems tend to be more resilient — when nothing is identical, no single shock takes it all. Monoculture is the engineered thing. Cavendish Space is our answer to it — caves, campfires, and watering holes for dandelions, tulips, and orchids alike. The Universe Runs on Difference · Stimpunks
