The deficit story reads the troughs as brokenness, measured against a smooth, standard line. But look again. The flat line is the Cavendish banana — the monoculture we were told to match. The spikes are the default state of matter: variety, the thing that actually makes something new. The peaks are real. So are the troughs. The mycelial network The oldest anarchist in the room Beneath the forest floor runs a living web of fungal threads — mycelium — laced through the soil and trading nutrients with the roots it meets. That trade is well established; how far the shared networks reach, and how much moves tree to tree through them, is still argued over by the people who dig them up. It has no head office. It grows in every direction at once, feeds its neighbors, and asks no one's permission. Its intelligence is distributed: problems get solved, paths get reinforced, weak connections fade — all with no commanding center telling each thread what to do. We know this shape, because it is how we try to hold each other. A competency network — everyone knowing something, sharing it with whoever needs it. Mutual aid — resources moving to where the need is greatest, not up a hierarchy to be rationed back down. Zero hierarchy is not a slogan we impose on the network. It is the shape the network takes when we stop forcing it into a chain of command. The mycelium never needed a manager. Neither, it turns out, do we — we need interdependence, which is a very different thing. no center trade distributed network · no commanding center hyphae · nodes · nutrient trade · reinforcing paths Underground · Stimpunks

The star-forged carbon of Bone Song does not stop at the skeleton. It falls, becomes soil, is taken up by the network, and passed along — star stuff all the way down, and up again through the ground. The poem Beneath the forest, a network with no name is doing the work. No head office. No throne. No plan on file. It grows in every direction at once, feeds its neighbors, and breaks the dead down into the living — underground, unseen, asking no one's permission. We know this shape. It is how we try to hold each other: no one at the center, resources moving to wherever the need is, everyone teaching, everyone learning, growth in every direction at once. Decomposition is not the end. Rock becomes soil. A fallen tree becomes a nursery. Nothing is wasted here — only waiting to be metabolized into whatever comes next. The carbon in you was forged in a star. It fell. It became soil. The network took it up and passed it on, and some of it became you. Star stuff, all the way down, and up again through the ground. The realest work happens in the dark, where no one is watching, where the metrics never reach. Do not mistake invisibility for absence. The network is busiest exactly where you cannot see it. We are not admiring a clever organism. We are kin, recognizing a relative. We look for ourselves in the fungi and we find us there: mischief with a purpose, refusing the world as given, making new possibilities while composting the old. We love you down to your star stuff — and up again through the soil. To the thread. To the trade. To the dark. To the network that occasionally surfaces and is busiest when it does not. L★S. What would you lose if you had to make it visible to count? On kinship — where do you see yourself in the mycelium, and what changes if you live as a network that occasionally surfaces rather than a self that occasionally connects? Underground is the fifth zine in the Stimpunks series — the below to Bone Song's above. It is offered freely, to be printed and folded and handed to someone who needs it. It draws on two Stimpunks pieces, "A Mycelium and a Rhizome" and "The Mycelial Worldview Is Punk," and on the sources they build from: the MOTH collective's essay "Punk Law: Lessons from Fungi," Toby Kiers and SPUN on "punk science," and the documentary Allpa Ukundi, Ñukanchi Pura (Kichwa for "underground, around, and among us"), made with the Kichwa people of Sarayaku in the Ecuadorian Amazon together with the Fungi Foundation and SPUN. The rhizome comes from Deleuze & Guattari; the neurodiversity paradigm language from Nick Walker and the Autistic community of InLv; the cosmology from Carl Sagan. The Stimpunks synthesis is our own extension, not a claim made by those authors. On the science: mycorrhizal symbiosis — fungi and roots trading nutrients — is well established. The popular "wood wide web" picture of forests wired together, with elder trees feeding seedlings through shared fungal networks, is contested; see Karst, Jones & Hoeksema, "Positive citation bias and overinterpreted results lead to misinformation on common mycorrhizal networks in forests" (Nature Ecology & Evolution 7, 2023). We keep the kinship and drop the overclaim. A rhyme, not a proof. The underground has been among us all along. The mycelial worldview is punk, and punk is a Stimpunks worldview. main sequence hot cool brightnessred dwarf L★S · 001 The Long Slow Burn Red dwarf · M-type main sequence ~0.1–0.6 solar masses · lives trillions of yrs The smallest, coolest, dimmest stars that still fuse hydrogen — and by far the most common stars there are. They burn so slowly they outlast every brilliant star, by a margin longer than the universe has yet existed. most common starslow burntrillions of yearsquiet endures ▸ Field notes Field notes · Red dwarf · M-type main sequence Red dwarfs are the smallest, coolest, dimmest stars that still fuse hydrogen — and they are by far the most common stars in the galaxy. Because they burn their fuel so slowly, and mix it so thoroughly, they last almost unimaginably long: many trillions of years, far longer than the current age of the universe. Not one red dwarf has ever died of old age, because there hasn't been time. Bright, fast, and spectacular is one way to be a star. Dim, slow, and enduring is another — and it's the way most stars actually take. Quiet and long outlasts loud and brief, every single time. Trait Sounds like Actually Dim and cool underpowered sips its fuel for trillions of years Small lesser the most common star in the galaxy Slow unremarkable outlasts every brilliant star Its way slow and long, not bright · L★S 001

main sequence hot cool brightnessfusion limitbrown dwarf L★S · 002 The So-Called Failure Brown dwarf · sub-stellar object ~13–80 Jupiter masses · no sustained fusion Forms like a star but never gathers quite enough mass to sustain hydrogen fusion — so astronomy calls it a "failed star." A strange verdict to hand an object for being exactly what it is. "failed star"below the linea real objectnamed for a lack ▸ Field notes Field notes · Brown dwarf · sub-stellar object Brown dwarfs form like stars but never gather quite enough mass to sustain hydrogen fusion in their cores, so astronomers have long called them "failed stars." It's a strange verdict to hand an object for existing exactly as it is. They glow for ages on their own warmth and a little early deuterium fusion, cooling slowly down through the infrared. The boundary between "star" and "failed star" sits around 8% of the Sun's mass — a real physical threshold, but the word failed is ours, not nature's. Below a line someone drew, a whole legitimate kind of object got named for what it isn't. We'd rather name it for what it is. Trait Sounds like Actually Never fused hydrogen a "failed star" a whole legitimate kind of object Below the mass line didn't make the cut the line is ours, not nature’s Cool and faint barely a star glows for ages on its own warmth Its way below the line we drew · L★S 002

main sequence hot cool brightnessvariable L★S · 003 Energy on Its Own Rhythm Variable star · e.g. Cepheid, Mira brightness cycles · hours to years A star whose brightness rises and falls on a cycle. Easy to read as a failure to hold steady — but the pulsing is how it works, and in the Cepheids, that very rhythm is how we measured the size of the universe. pulsingnot unstablea built-in rhythmmeasures the cosmos ▸ Field notes Field notes · Variable star · e.g. Cepheid, Mira Variable stars don't hold a steady brightness; they swell and shrink, brighten and dim, on cycles from hours to years. It would be easy to read that as instability — a failure to keep it together. But the pulsing is not a malfunction. It's how these stars work, a rhythm built into their very structure. And that rhythm turned out to be one of the most useful things in all of astronomy: Cepheid variables pulse with a period that reveals their true brightness, which let Henrietta Leavitt — and everyone since — measure distances clear across the cosmos. Energy that comes and goes on its own cycle isn't lesser. Here, it's how we learned the size of the universe. Trait Sounds like Actually Brightness rises and falls can't hold steady pulses on a reliable cycle Never constant unstable the change is how it works Its fluctuation a defect how we measure the whole universe Its way rhythmic, not constant · L★S 003

main sequence hot cool brightnesspulsar L★S · 004 The Precise Signal Pulsar · rotating neutron star spins up to ~700×/second · ms-precise The collapsed core of a dead massive star — a Sun's mass in a city-sized sphere — spinning fast and sweeping a beam past us like a lighthouse, with a regularity that rivals atomic clocks. neutron starmillisecond precisiontiny, densea galactic clock ▸ Field notes Field notes · Pulsar · rotating neutron star A pulsar is a neutron star — the collapsed core of a dead massive star, a whole Sun's worth of mass packed into a sphere the size of a city — spinning fast and sweeping a beam of radiation past us like a lighthouse. Some spin over 700 times a second, and their pulses arrive with a regularity that rivals atomic clocks. Small, dense, easy to overlook, and quietly one of the most precise things in the universe. Astronomers use pulsars to navigate, to test gravity, to hunt for gravitational waves. A tremendous, exact signal in a tiny package the eye would never notice. Trait Sounds like Actually Tiny and dense collapsed, spent a city-sized cosmic clock Spins wildly out of control keeps time to the millisecond Faint to the eye insignificant its beam sweeps the galaxy Its way precise, not spent · L★S 004

main sequence hot cool brightnessbinary L★S · 005 Never Alone Binary system · two or more stars ~half of Sun-like stars have a partner We picture stars as solitary, but roughly half of Sun-like stars — and most massive ones — live bound to a companion, orbiting a shared centre, sometimes trading mass across the gap. Shaped by relationship, not in spite of it. pairedrelationalshared orbitmost of the sky ▸ Field notes Field notes · Binary system · two or more stars We picture stars as solitary points of light, but roughly half of all Sun-like stars — and most massive ones — live bound to at least one companion, orbiting a shared centre of gravity, sometimes trading streams of matter across the space between them. A star's whole life can be shaped by the one it circles. Being paired isn't a lesser or dependent way to exist; for most stars, it's simply the ordinary one. Identity here is relational — what a star becomes depends on who it's with. Most of the sky was never single. Trait Sounds like Actually Not solitary dependent most stars live bound to another Shares mass and orbit entangled shaped by relationship, not despite it Two, not one incomplete alone a system, whole together Its way relational, not solitary · L★S 005

main sequence hot cool brightnessred giant L★S · 006 A Later Way of Being Red giant · late-life phase what the Sun becomes in ~5 billion yrs When a Sun-like star spends the hydrogen in its core, it doesn't fail — it transforms: swelling huge, cooling to deep red, and forging heavier elements it sheds into space to seed new worlds. Change, not decline. transformedoff the main sequenceforges elementsnot decline ▸ Field notes Field notes · Red giant · late-life phase When a Sun-like star exhausts the hydrogen in its core, it doesn't fail — it transforms. It swells enormously, its surface cools to a deep red, and it begins fusing heavier elements, forging carbon and oxygen and shedding them into space where they'll seed new worlds. In about five billion years, this is what our own Sun will become. It's tempting to call that decline. But the red giant is the same star living a different phase — larger, cooler, and doing some of the most generative work of its whole existence. Aging, here, is not diminishment. It's another way of being — and a fertile one. Trait Sounds like Actually Left the main sequence past its prime entered a new phase, not a decline Swollen and cooler falling apart forging the elements of new life Utterly changed no longer itself the same star, living differently Its way transformed, not declined · L★S 006

main sequence hot cool brightnesswhite dwarf L★S · 007 The Long Afterward White dwarf · stellar remnant Earth-sized · a teaspoon weighs tonnes What remains after a red giant sheds its outer layers: the exposed core, a Sun's mass packed into the size of Earth. It fuses nothing anymore — and shines on, on stored heat alone, for billions upon billions of years. remnantstopped fusingstill shiningan enduring end ▸ Field notes Field notes · White dwarf · stellar remnant After a red giant sheds its outer layers, what remains is a white dwarf: the exposed core, roughly the mass of the Sun packed into the size of the Earth, so dense that a teaspoon of it would weigh tonnes. It no longer fuses anything. And yet it shines — on stored heat alone — for billions upon billions of years as it slowly cools. We tend to file "stopped working" under "finished." The white dwarf declines the framing. Its fusing life is over, and it goes on glowing longer than most stars ever live: a quiet, luminous afterward that is still, unmistakably, a way of being a star. Trait Sounds like Actually Stopped fusing dead shines on for billions of years Small and faint finished the enduring core, cooling slowly An end-state nothing left a quiet, luminous afterward Its way enduring, not ended · L★S 007

main sequence hot cool brightnessblue giant L★S · 008 Bright and Brief Blue giant · O/B-type supergiant tens of solar masses · gone in millions of yrs The showpieces — tens of times the Sun's mass, blazing hot and staggeringly bright. If brightness were the measure, these would win. But they burn out in a cosmic instant, and they're the rarest stars of all. brilliantfast-burningrarestnot the standard ▸ Field notes Field notes · Blue giant · O/B-type supergiant Blue giants and supergiants are the showpieces — tens of times the Sun's mass, blazing hot and staggeringly luminous. If brightness were the measure of a star, these would win outright. But they pay for it: they tear through their fuel and live only a few million years, a cosmic instant, before dying as supernovae. It's worth noticing which way of being a star we're tempted to call the "best" — the brilliant, fast-burning one — and then noticing that it's the rarest and shortest-lived of them all. Brightness was never the measure. It's one way among many, and far from the way most stars go. Stimpunks Foundation · Community Reader We Are All Star Stuff Zine No. 4 · In progress Open call for contributors The first three zines in this series made arguments. This one holds space for something different: the actual voices of the people the series is for. Zines No. 1, 2, and 3 built the framework — the piezoelectric bones, the cosmology of care, the neurodiversity paradigm. They explained why you are made of star stuff and why that matters. We Are All Star Stuff is the zine that asks: what does that mean to you? We're collecting short pieces — a few sentences to a few paragraphs — from Autistic, ADHD, dyslexic, disabled, and otherwise neurodivergent people, and from the family members, educators, and community members who love them. No expertise required. No particular format. Just your honest answer to the question of what it means to be loved down to your star stuff, or to love someone that way. This zine will be offered freely, the same as the rest of the series — print-at-home, shareable, open edition. Every contributor will be credited exactly as they choose: full name, first name only, initials, role, or anonymous. Prompts You don't need to answer any of these directly — they're starting points, not requirements. Write toward whatever feels true. "When I first encountered the phrase 'Love You Down To Your Star Stuff' — or the idea behind it — something shifted. Here's what shifted, and why." "The neurodiversity paradigm says my neurological difference is variation, not deficit. Here's what that reframe has meant in practice — in my life, my work, my relationships, my sense of myself." "Here's a moment when I felt — or gave — the kind of love that goes all the way in. Past the hard parts. Down to the star stuff." "The idea that the universe doesn't pathologize its own variation: here's what that means to me, or what I wish it had meant to someone in my life earlier." "Something I want other neurodivergent people — or the people who love them — to know. Anything. L★S." Format Length A few sentences to a few paragraphs. No minimum, no hard maximum — but shorter pieces are easier to fit and we'll work with you on longer ones. Form Prose, fragment, list, letter, poem — any form that fits what you want to say. Write in your own voice. Formal or casual, both welcome. Credit You choose: full name, first name, initials, role ("an Autistic parent"), or anonymous. You can also add a brief bio line if you'd like. Edits We'll share any edits with you before publication and won't change your words without your approval. Rights You keep all rights to your words. We ask for permission to include your piece in this zine and future print editions of it, nothing more. Deadline No hard deadline yet. We'll publish when we have enough voices to fill a zine. Earlier submissions mean earlier inclusion. A note on anonymity: You're welcome to share as much or as little about yourself as you want. You don't need to disclose a diagnosis, a label, or a relationship. If you want to write "someone who has been loved this way" and nothing more, that's a complete and welcome contribution. L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff Send your piece → stimpunks@stimpunks.org Questions before submitting? Same address. Or reach us through stimpunks.org/contact. 11 Guest Zine Stimpunks Foundation · Guest Zine · No. 11 Why Difference Comes First Inspired by our collaborative Stimpunks work, and my own neuroqueering Deleuze project, I've been thinking about the connections in-between — physics, philosophy, my own life as an Autistic person. This is me following that thread. Helen Edgar · Autistic Realms · More Realms L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · guest edition ·

Two · I'm not a fixed thing I'm not a fixed thing A little while back I wrote about something called relational quantum mechanics — a way of thinking about physics where tiny particles don't have fixed qualities all on their own. They only become something in relation to whatever's around them (Rovelli, 1996). I'm not a physicist — it's one idea among several, and physicists argue about it. As a multiply neurodivergent person, that's always been closer to how I experience myself — not as a fixed, separate thing moving through the world, but as something that shows up through my relationships and encounters with everything around me (Edgar, 2026a). I'm still working through what that means. Physics, philosophy, and my own life keep circling the same ideas about being interconnected, unfixed, always transforming. Why Difference Comes First · Helen Edgar

Three · my monotropic galaxy My monotropic galaxy The oldest light we can see is called the cosmic microwave background — it's the afterglow of the Big Bang, and it's almost perfectly smooth. It only varies by about one part in 100,000 across the whole sky — almost uniform, but only almost. Those tiny variations — slightly denser here, slightly thinner there — were the beginning of everything. Gravity pulled the denser bits together, and over billions of years they became stars, galaxies, planets, you, me, all of it. If the universe really had been perfectly uniform, it would have stayed a flat, empty fog forever. Nothing to see, no one to see it. Structure only exists because that near-sameness broke. That's the same shape I recognise in my own monotropic attention — energy pulled gravitationally into a few bright points, rather than spread out in an even, undifferentiated glow. And yet it's exactly that unevenness, that refusal to flatten, that so many of us — anyone who's ever been called too much, not enough, or too different — have been measured against. the "almost" is where everything comes from almost uniform · not quite the tiny unevenness seeds the stars Why Difference Comes First · Helen Edgar

Four · neuronormative time Measured against neuronormative time I've spent a lot of my life being measured against a flat line. Nobody always said it in those words, but that's what was happening — a standard chart, a "typical" way of communicating or paying attention or experiencing the world, treated as the baseline everyone should be smoothed toward. And me, positioned as the deviation that needed explaining, or fixing, or at least accounting for. That flat line was never just about behaviour — it was also about time: a single approved tempo, a single approved rhythm, everyone expected to arrive and finish and transition together, in step with a clock that was never actually neutral. So there's something that genuinely steadies me in learning that the universe itself never once managed that. what was already there, moving the "typical" baseline you = "deviation" a straight line, laid over what was already moving the grid comes after the field, not before Uniformity was never the achievement. It's the thing that would have stopped everything before it even started. Why Difference Comes First · Helen Edgar

Five · no normal or baseline There is no normal or baseline Gilles Deleuze, working with Félix Guattari, made a version of this same argument. Deleuze noticed that a lot of Western thinking treats difference as secondary — judged by how much it resembles some ideal, some average, some "normal" category. All of that quietly assumes the baseline came first, and difference is just a deviation from it. The baseline is the thing that got built. The idea of normality is what has shaped our capitalist society (Chapman, 2023) and is what we are judged against (Deleuze, 1994). Difference is what's actually there, first — and identity is what eventually forms out of it, temporarily and locally, the way a crystal settles out of a solution along the gaps and spaces in between — the places where those of us most marginalised live, and where we build our own networks, our own solidarity. This is where Deleuze and Guattari's idea of smooth space becomes useful (Deleuze & Guattari, 1987). Smooth space is full of local, variable difference — it hasn't had a fixed grid laid over it yet. Striated space is what happens when that grid arrives: when a field gets measured, divided, standardised. Difference doesn't get smoothed into existence by that process. Smoothing is what a system does afterward, only if it insists on it — striation laid over what was already smooth. Nothing gets smoothed into existence. Smoothing is what happens to something afterward — only if a system insists on it. Why Difference Comes First · Helen Edgar

Six · smooth ≠ flat Smooth doesn't mean flat Smooth space isn't empty of movement — it's just ungridded. It cuts against how regulation usually gets talked about, as though it means being still, quiet, zen: a flat line of its own. But smooth space is defined by what it lacks — a grid — not by what it's doing. It can be full of movement and still be smooth — which is closer to how neurodivergent regulation actually works: through stimming, through bodily autonomy, through movement rather than stillness. That's closer to what I recognise when I try to describe my own attention — my porousness to my environment, the way my sensory system stays open to everything around it, the way time folds back on itself instead of running in a straight line. Not flat. Not gridded. Full of shape that never quite resolves into one measurable thing. SMOOTH · ungridded STRIATED · gridded smooth is not empty · it's ungridded the fog was neither — a field before either one Why Difference Comes First · Helen Edgar

Seven · ethodiversity What ethodiversity means This is where Ombre Tarragnat's work on ethodiversity has become important to me. Ethodiversity is the variety of ways of being and behaving, across humans and other animals — and Tarragnat is precise about where it actually lives: not inside any one person, but as a property of the relationships between us, the way biodiversity belongs to a whole ecosystem, not to any single creature in it (Tarragnat, 2025). Ethonormativity, in their framing, is the unwritten rule about which ways of being are allowed to count as normal in a given room. Put next to Deleuze, I don't think it's a stretch to say ethonormativity simply is that grid — applied to how we're allowed to behave. A fixed grid laid over a field that was already full of variation before the grid ever showed up. Ethonormativity reaches further than neuronormativity, though. Neuronormativity is about which neurotypes get treated as the default — Autistic brains judged against non-Autistic ones, for instance. Ethonormativity is the wider grid underneath that: it governs which ways of being and behaving, across every species, get to count as acceptable at all. It holds neuronormativity inside it, but it isn't limited to brains, or even to humans (Tarragnat, 2025). Ethonormativity simply is that grid — a fixed grid laid over a field that was already full of variation before the grid ever showed up. Why Difference Comes First · Helen Edgar

Eight · a constellation of intensities A constellation of intensities I recognise that grid in every space I've ever masked in — education, the workplace, wherever something that was moving gets asked to hold still long enough to be measured. And I recognise its absence, with real gratitude, in the spaces I'm part of — NeuroHub Community and David Gray-Hammond, Stimpunks: an Autistic rhizome, a mycelial network of care, non-hierarchical, no fixed centre, connecting wherever it meets (Deleuze & Guattari, 1987). I used to think the shape of my own mind was something like a spiky profile — a way of picturing uneven ability across different areas, real peaks and real troughs, instead of one flat line running across the whole of who you are. At least it's truer than a flat line. But a profile still measures. It still needs axes, still has edges — and that's exactly where I want to push further, past even the spiky profile. What I actually recognise, when I try to map myself, isn't a chart at all. It's a constellation of intensities: a galaxy, always in relationship with itself, always in motion, never finished (Edgar, 2026b). Some stars I've lived in for decades. Others I've only just learned to name. None of them sit on an axis. They just belong to the same galaxy — we are all made of stardust. flat line a grid spiky profile still axes, still edges a constellation no axis · in motion flat line → spiky profile → no chart at all even the spiky profile is still a grid A profile still measures. It still needs axes, still has edges. What I actually recognise, when I try to map myself, isn't a chart at all. Why Difference Comes First · Helen Edgar

Nine · permission The universe doesn't do flat lines I still don't have this fully settled or finished. But every time I follow this thread — from the sky, down through physics and philosophy, into the actual shape of my own attention — I end up in the same place. Not a tidy conclusion. More like a kind of permission. The universe doesn't do flat lines. It never really tried to. It went straight from near-uniform fog to unrepeatable structure, without ever pausing at sameness for its own sake. I think that's worth remembering, gently — the next time any of us is asked to explain why we don't match the line. We are all star dust. We are neuroqueering the spiky profile: no edges, limitless ways of being. Why Difference Comes First · Helen Edgar

L★S · 001 The Inner Ocean Europa · moon of Jupiter a global ocean under ~15–25 km of ice A quiet, cracked marble of ice on the outside — and underneath, a global ocean of liquid salt water, possibly holding more water than all of Earth's seas combined. Kept warm by tides, not sunlight. inner oceantidal heatunder icemaybe life ▸ Field notes Field notes · Europa · moon of Jupiter Europa looks, from outside, like a still, cracked marble of ice. Underneath is one of the most exciting places in the solar system: a global ocean of liquid salt water, kept warm not by sunlight but by the constant tidal flexing of Jupiter's gravity kneading the moon's interior. There may be more water there than in all of Earth's oceans combined. No sky, no sun — no problem. The warmth comes from within, and the seafloor may host the same kind of chemistry that feeds life around Earth's deep-sea vents. A still surface is not an empty one. Some of the richest worlds keep the whole ocean on the inside. Earth's rule Its own rule The result warmth from the Sun warmth from tidal flexing a warm ocean in the dark oceans on the surface ocean sealed under ice ~2× Earth's water, hidden life needs sunlight chemistry at the seafloor a real candidate for life Runs on tidal heat, not sunlight · L★S 001

L★S · 002 The Other Chemistry Titan · moon of Saturn methane rain · −179°C · thick orange haze Titan runs Earth's whole weather system with the labels swapped: clouds, rain, rivers, and seas — of liquid methane, under an orange haze, where water ice is as hard as rock. A world that senses on a different chemistry. methane seasorange hazeother chemistrya full water cycle ▸ Field notes Field notes · Titan · moon of Saturn Titan runs Earth's weather system with the labels swapped. It has clouds, rain, rivers, lakes, and seas — but made of liquid methane and ethane, beneath a thick orange haze, at −179°C where water ice is as hard as granite. It is the only place besides Earth we know of with stable liquid on its surface. It senses and moves through the world on a different chemistry entirely. To call it inhospitable is really just to say it isn't Earth. On its own terms it is complete: a full hydrologic cycle, a landscape carved by flowing liquid, a sky with its own weather. A different medium, a different light, a whole world getting on with it. Earth's rule Its own rule The result rain is water rain is methane rivers and seas of hydrocarbons a clear blue sky a thick orange haze a different light to sense by water flows, rock is solid methane flows, ice is bedrock the same cycle, other materials Runs on methane, not water · L★S 002

L★S · 003 What Has to Come Out Enceladus · moon of Saturn geysers venting to space · ~500 km wide A small, bright moon that cannot keep its ocean to itself. From cracks at its south pole it fires plumes of water vapour hundreds of kilometres into space — and that spray is how we learned what its hidden sea contains. plumeshidden oceanexpressiontasted from space ▸ Field notes Field notes · Enceladus · moon of Saturn Enceladus is a small, brilliant-white moon that cannot keep its ocean to itself. From four warm cracks at its south pole — the "tiger stripes" — it fires enormous plumes of water vapour and ice grains hundreds of kilometres up, straight into space, feeding one of Saturn's rings. The Cassini spacecraft flew through the spray and sampled the sea without ever landing. There's something to love in a world whose inner life simply has to come out — and whose expression turned out to be exactly how we learned what it holds. What it couldn't contain is what let us know it was there. L★S · 004 Another Orientation Uranus · seventh planet axial tilt ~98° · orbiting on its side Every other planet spins more or less upright. Uranus is tipped almost completely onto its side, rolling around the Sun like a marble. Not broken — oriented differently, and completing its long orbit perfectly well that way. sidewaystilted ~98°rolls, not spinsnot broken ▸ Field notes Field notes · Uranus · seventh planet Every other planet spins more or less upright. Uranus is tipped almost completely onto its side — an axial tilt of about 98° — so it rolls around the Sun like a marble instead of spinning like a top. Its poles take turns pointing nearly straight at the Sun, giving each one roughly 42 years of continuous daylight followed by 42 years of night. It isn't broken; it's oriented differently, and it completes its long orbit perfectly well that way. Most likely knocked sideways by an ancient collision, it simply kept going on a new axis. Same Sun, same orbit — another way of facing it. L★S · 005 The World With No Exit Venus · second planet ~465°C surface · 92× Earth's pressure Nearly Earth's twin in size, born next door — but its thick carbon-dioxide air traps heat it can't release. A runaway greenhouse near 465°C. The hard part isn't the heat; it's having nowhere for the pressure to go. runaway greenhouseno releasetrapped heatthe cost of no exit ▸ Field notes Field notes · Venus · second planet Venus and Earth are nearly the same size and were born right next door to each other. But Venus's thick carbon-dioxide atmosphere traps the Sun's heat and can't let it go — a runaway greenhouse that holds the surface near 465°C, hot enough to melt lead, under pressure about ninety times Earth's. The hard part of Venus isn't the heat itself; it's having no way to release it. We'd read that gently, and at the level of systems, not selves: what a world — or a room, or a life — needs isn't only less coming in, but somewhere for the pressure to go. The lesson of Venus is an argument for exits: for relief, for cool-down, for a way out. Systems with no release run away. So build the exit. Pluto met two parts but not the third — it hasn't "cleared its orbital neighbourhood," since it shares its region with other icy bodies — and was reclassified as a dwarf planet. Nothing about Pluto changed: same world, same orbit, same slow, heart-shaped plain of frozen nitrogen. Only the category moved. That's the whole of it, and it rhymes with The Lines We Drew: a definition is a human decision — useful, and revisable — not a fact discovered in the rock. You can redraw the line around something and change nothing about the thing itself. Pluto is exactly what it always was. still being woven 28 Wyrd Stimpunks Foundation · Guest Zine · No. 28 Wyrd & Weird on the old word for fate, and the newer word we made of it Helen Edgar · Autistic Realms · a becoming, not a verdict L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·

Before the insult The word before the insult Long before "weird" meant strange, it meant becoming. In Old English, wyrd comes from weorþan — "to happen, to occur, to become" (Stone, 2022). It wasn't a synonym for doom, and it wasn't a script waiting to be read out. It was the word for the process by which anything at all comes into being. A person's wyrd wasn't what had been written about them. It was what they were still becoming. The same root gives us a second thread worth holding onto: Old English wyrd is twined with the ancestors of modern "worth" (Stone, 2022). Becoming and worth, tangled in the same word, from the start. "Weird" isn't the opposite of normal. It's the oldest word we have for becoming. one root, two threads weorþan "to become" wyrd becoming worth value becoming & worth, from the start tangled in one word Wyrd & Weird · Helen Edgar

an account, not a plot Urð has come to be Verðandi becoming Skuld what is owed the well beneath Yggdrasill what is, what becomes, what is owed The well beneath the tree Worth, not written Norse tradition keeps fate's three keepers at a well beneath the world tree, Yggdrasill — Urð, Verðandi, and Skuld. Popular retellings gloss them as past, present, and future. That's tidy, and it isn't quite right (Stone, 2022). Verðandi comes from verða, "to become." Skuld means "debt" or "tax." Urð may share a root with worth, or with a word meaning "to turn." Read plainly, together they describe not a plot but an account: what has come to be, what is happening now, and what is owed simply for having lived (Stone, 2022). A life's wyrd was never a plot laid down before you were born. It was the worth a life comes to have, built thread by thread in the living of it. — reading Stone (2022), pp. 36–37 Wyrd & Weird · Helen Edgar

Weaving, not writing The web, not the line Fate's keepers — the nornir, the Moirai, the Weird Sisters — are pictured again and again as spinners and weavers, working at a loom whose cloth is called, in one Old English poem, "the web of man" (Stone, 2022). Notice the shape of that image. Fate was never drawn as a single straight line running from birth to death. It was drawn as cloth — many threads, crossing, holding each other's weight, none of them load-bearing alone. A single thread can be cut. A web asks a different question: whose hands are helping hold it up? A line has one direction. A web holds weight from every side. a line one cut ends it a web holds from every side cloth, not a single strand many hands, many threads Wyrd & Weird · Helen Edgar

the three who spun it picked up again, as a name nornir · Moirai · the Weird Sisters impossible to write out How the word survived Weird Sisters, reclaimed Wyrd stayed alive in English through women who unsettled people. Medieval, mostly Christian, writers kept the word for fate but let the goddess behind it quietly fade (Stone, 2022). By Shakespeare, they were the three Weird Sisters of Macbeth, drawn from Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) — feared, consulted, impossible to write out of the story. A small honest note: Shakespeare's First Folio actually prints "weyward sisters." "Weird" is Holinshed's own word for them, fixed in place by later editors — which, if anything, makes the thread back to wyrd even more direct. Centuries on, "weird" drifted again — from fate-word, to uncanny, to a casual insult for anything too strange to sit comfortably in the room. Autistic and disabled communities didn't start that drift. But plenty of us have chosen to run it backward: to pick "weird" up again as a name, not a verdict. That's not just cheek. It's etymologically honest. We're not turning a slur into a compliment — we're giving an old, powerful word its meaning back. Wyrd & Weird · Helen Edgar

Held with care What wyrd is not Reclaiming a word means being clear about what we are not saying with it. Nota script written before you arrived, with no part in it for you to weave. Notdoom. Skuld's debt is the cost of having lived — not a punishment for how you lived it. Nota synonym for wrong, broken, too much, or not enough. Notsomething done to you alone. A web has many hands on it. many hands on it no thread load-bearing alone a web, not a single strand whose hands help hold it? Wyrd & Weird · Helen Edgar

still on the loom unfinished — and that is the design the cloth is still being made nobody is finished The root, again Becoming, together Weorþan — the root under wyrd — never meant "to be." It meant "to become." The self it describes isn't a fixed thing waiting at the end of a life; it's a self still happening, still owed, still worth building (Stone, 2022). That's a strange kind of comfort, if you've ever been told your difference makes you incomplete, or unfinished, or not-yet-normal. Under the old word, nobody is finished. Becoming was never a flaw in the design. It was the design. Nobody is finished. Becoming was never the flaw. It was the design. Wyrd & Weird · Helen Edgar

Wyrd & Weird is a guest zine in the Stimpunks Star Stuff series, written by Helen Edgar (Autistic Realms) — neuro-affirming, identity-first, written for the community. With the Wikipedia entries on Wyrd and the Three Witches (retrieved July 2026). This zine paraphrases and cites Stone's research throughout; no passages are reproduced from the book. The reading — wyrd and weird as a shared word for becoming, worth, and weaving, and the case for reclaiming "weird" as identity — is Helen's own. 7 Never One Thing Stimpunks Foundation · Zine No. 7 You Were Never One Thing on endosymbiosis, the cell as a truce, and interdependence written into the body L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·

Endosymbiosis The stranger that stayed More than one and a half billion years ago, a free-living bacterium ended up inside a larger cell — and was not digested. It stayed. It became the mitochondrion, the part that powers almost everything you do. And it never quite stopped being itself: it still keeps its own loop of DNA, its own ribosomes, and it divides on its own schedule. New mitochondria come only from old ones. Every complex cell you have carries that ancient merger, trillions of times over. You are not a single thing that happens to contain parts. You are the parts, still in their long agreement. host cell nucleus mitochondrion its own DNA a cell that is also a settlement host cell · engulfed bacterium · genome retained You Were Never One Thing · Stimpunks

lichen fungus + alga = one : gut microbiome ≈ 38 trillion : 30 trillion microbe : human cells mycorrhiza plant root + fungus the merger was never a one-off symbiosis, woven through the tree of life Cooperation, over and over Not a footnote. An engine. The mitochondrion was not a fluke. The green in every leaf — the chloroplast — came from a separate merger, when a cell took in a photosynthesizing cyanobacterium and kept it. A lichen is a fungus and an alga living as one body. Most land plants feed through fungi laced into their roots. And your own gut carries roughly as many bacterial cells as human ones — about thirty-eight trillion to thirty. Cooperation is not a footnote to competition. It is one of the engines that built complex life at all. We are not individuals who sometimes team up. We are teams that learned to say I. You Were Never One Thing · Stimpunks

The poem More than a billion years ago, one small cell ended up inside another and was not digested. It stayed. It became the mitochondrion — the thing that powers you now — and it never stopped being itself. Its own loop of DNA. Its own clock. A guest that became a home. You are not one thing. You are a truce so old it forgot it was ever two, kept alive in every cell, trillions of times over. This is not a metaphor we reached for. It is the blueprint. The body is a settlement. The self is a collaboration that learned to answer to one name. So when they told you to stand on your own, to need no one, to be independent or be nothing — they were telling a story over a body that had already decided otherwise, a billion years before you were born. You were never one thing. You were never alone in there. We love you down to the merger, down to the two that became you, down to the star stuff that both of them were made of. L★S. Autonomy wasnever the sameas being alone

The reframe Autonomy was never the same as being alone Disability justice values interdependence over independence. Your own cells settle the argument. "Independence" was always a story told over a body that is itself a collaboration — a merger it never dissolved. Needing support is not a failure of selfhood. Selfhood is need met by need. The mitochondrion did not lose itself by depending on the cell, and the cell did not lose itself by depending back. That mutual keeping is what made something new possible. You were never meant to do this on your own. Nothing complex ever was. What this is not Notwe're all one, so your specific needs dissolve. Each partner kept its own genome — difference is the point. Notso merge in, mask, disappear into the group. The mitochondrion stayed itself inside the whole. Nota tidy metaphor for corporate "synergy." This is bodies and survival, not a mission statement. Notinterdependence as a softer word for forced dependence. It is reciprocal, or it is not this. Nota diagnosis, or a claim that any body is broken or in need of repair. Endosymbiosis builds every complex cell alive — yours included, exactly as it is. You were never one thing. So you were never truly alone — not even at the level of a single cell. If needing support is not a failure of selfhood but its actual structure, what changes about how you ask, and how you give? You Were Never One Thing is the seventh zine in the Stimpunks series, and a companion to Bone Song — Bone Song was the skeleton; this is the cell. The science is established. Mitochondria descend from once-free-living bacteria (alphaproteobacteria) that took up residence inside an ancient host cell — most likely an archaeon — more than one and a half billion years ago; the exact timing is still debated. Mitochondria keep their own DNA and divide on their own schedule. Chloroplasts arose from a separate endosymbiosis of cyanobacteria. The gut carries roughly as many bacterial cells as human cells — about 38 trillion to 30 trillion (Sender, Fuchs & Milo, 2016), correcting the old 10:1 figure. Serial endosymbiotic theory was given its modern form by Lynn Margulis (as Lynn Sagan) in "On the Origin of Mitosing Cells" (1967), reviving earlier proposals by Mereschkowsky and Wallin; phylogenomics has since confirmed its core. The reading — interdependence over independence, autonomy was never the same as being alone — is ours. The atoms of both ancient partners were forged in stars. Cooperation runs all the way down to star stuff.
